docs.title: Introduction to AtDork
docs.text:
Welcome to the official documentation for AtDork, a professional Open Source Intelligence (OSINT) and advanced dorking tool engineered for security researchers, penetration testers, and bug bounty hunters.

AtDork automates the extraction of exposed documents, vulnerable parameters, misconfigured server indexes, and leaked credentials from public search engine indexing.

docs.title: Why AtDork?
docs.text:
Unlike conventional dorking scripts that easily trigger captchas and face IP bans, AtDork incorporates sophisticated engineering principles to guarantee high availability and evasion:

  • Blazing Fast Parallelism – Highly optimized multi-threaded processing with configurable concurrency limits.
  • Multi-Engine Aggregator – Queries DuckDuckGo, Google, Bing, Startpage, Yandex, Yahoo, and more.
  • Ironclad Anonymity – Native Tor integration, persistent proxy rotation pools, and --ip-guard to prevent identity leaks.
  • Intelligent Resilience – Built-in circuit breakers, adaptive jitter delays, and error classification algorithms.
  • Seamless Pipelines – Directly pipe discovered endpoints into vulnerability scanners like wpscan or sqlmap.
  • Template System – YAML-based dork collections with {target} substitution and selective execution.
  • Dork Package Manager – atdork search / install / update over 994,600+ dorks in Atdork-DB — 123 dork packages across 31 @folders, plus 7 installable @plugins/ tools — all browsable in the web catalog.
  • Workflow Engine – Sequential multi-step dork campaigns in YAML: threshold-triggered retries, worker pools, guarded outputs, resumable state (atdork workflow run, --run-workflow).
  • Plugin System – Install extra Python tools from Atdork-DB (atdork install @plugins/<tool>), a git repo, a .py URL or your own registry (--source); each surfaces as --<plugin>-<option> flags (--dorkbuilder-text "…").
  • Watch Mode – Cron-friendly monitoring: atdork watch add + watch run re-runs dorks and reports only new findings (webhook alerts via --notify).
  • Docker Ready – Official image ghcr.io/amnottdevv/atdork ships the CLI and the full database — zero setup (Docker).

docs.title: Quick Stats
docs.text:
• 994,600+ Dorks – Across 123 packages in 31 themed @folders, refreshed weekly (web catalog).
  • 50+ CLI Flags – Complete control over every aspect of your search.
  • 6+ Search Engines – DuckDuckGo, Google, Bing, Startpage, Yandex, Yahoo.
  • 3 API Providers – Serper.dev, SerpApi and Brave Search API via engines: in atdork.yml.
  • 565 Unit Tests – Production-ready stability and reliability, run on Python 3.10 / 3.12 / 3.14.
  • 10+ Templates – Pre-built dork collections for SQLi, XSS, WordPress, and more.

Ethical Use

AtDork is intended for legal, authorized security testing only. You must have explicit written permission from the target owner before scanning. Unauthorized access to systems or data is strictly prohibited.

docs.title: Get Started
docs.text:
Ready to start? Run your first search now:

pip install atdork                          # install the CLI
git clone https://github.com/amnottdevv/Atdork-DB.git ~/Atdork-DB   # dork data (once)
atdork -q "site:gov filetype:pdf" -r 10     # first search

Or use Docker — no Python or clone needed:

docker run --rm -it ghcr.io/amnottdevv/atdork:latest -q "site:gov filetype:pdf" -r 10

Explore the Quick Start guide for a step-by-step tutorial, browse the dork packages in the web catalog, or dive into the Dork Database workflow.

docs.title: Basic Usage
docs.text:
This guide covers the most common AtDork commands you'll use daily. Whether you're a security researcher, bug bounty hunter, or OSINT practitioner, these examples will help you get started quickly.

All examples assume you have AtDork installed. If not, see Installation.

docs.title: Your First Search
docs.text:
The simplest command — search for PDF files on government websites:

atdork -q "site:gov filetype:pdf" -r 10
  • -q — your search query (dork)
  • -r 10 — return up to 10 results

docs.title: 1. Find Exposed Documents
docs.text:
# PDF files on government sites
atdork -q "site:gov filetype:pdf" -r 20

# Excel files on educational sites
atdork -q "site:edu filetype:xls" -r 20

# Config files with passwords
atdork -q 'filetype:env "DB_PASSWORD"' -r 20

docs.title: 2. Find Exposed Panels & Logins
docs.text:
# Admin login pages
atdork -q "inurl:admin login" -r 20

# phpMyAdmin consoles
atdork -q "intitle:phpmyadmin inurl:index.php" -r 20

docs.title: 3. Find Open Directories
docs.text:
# Directory indexing
atdork -q 'intitle:"index of" "backup"' -r 20

docs.title: Output Formats
docs.text:
Write results to disk in the format that fits your pipeline:

# JSON — for programmatic processing
atdork -q "site:example.com" --format json -o results.json

# CSV — for spreadsheets
atdork -q "site:example.com" --format csv -o results.csv

# Plain text (default)
atdork -q "site:example.com" -o results.txt

# One file per query in a directory
atdork --batch-file dorks.txt --output-dir ./results

docs.title: Batch Processing
docs.text:
Feed a whole list of dorks at once — one per line:

cat > dorks.txt << 'EOF'
site:edu filetype:xls
inurl:admin login
intitle:"index of" "backup"
EOF

atdork --batch-file dorks.txt -r 20 --format json --output-dir ./out

Use -v to stream results to the terminal while the batch runs.

docs.title: Dork Packages (Atdork-DB)
docs.text: Since v1.3.9.7 the dork data lives in the Atdork-DB repository — 123 packages across 31 @folders, ~994,600 dorks — managed by the built-in package manager. Browse the web catalog →

docs.title: Search the index
docs.text:
atdork search shodan         # packages mentioning "shodan"
atdork index                 # full package listing with descriptions

docs.title: Install packages
docs.text:
atdork install @cve/cve_1.txt     # canonical ref: folder + file
atdork install c@cve_1.txt        # shorthand (unique folder prefix)
atdork install @ghdb              # entire folder
atdork installed                  # list what's in ~/.atdork/packages
atdork uninstall @ghdb/01_footholds

docs.title: Run installed packages as queries
docs.text:
# Installed packages work as batch files
atdork --batch-file c@cve_1.txt -r 20

# Or load any ref straight from the database root (no install step)
atdork --database-dork @ghdb/01_footholds -r 20

# Preview without running
atdork --database-dork @cve --database-preview

# Random sample from a folder (deterministic with a seed)
atdork --database-dork @cms --database-r 50 --database-seed 7

# List everything available
atdork --list-database-dork

docs.title: Keep the data fresh
docs.text:
atdork update      # git pull --ff-only on the Atdork-DB checkout

Full ref grammar, folder list and category guides: Dork Database.

docs.title: Run with Docker
docs.text:
The official image bundles the CLI and the full database — no Python or clone needed:

docker pull ghcr.io/amnottdevv/atdork:latest

# Search
docker run --rm -it ghcr.io/amnottdevv/atdork:latest -q "site:gov filetype:pdf" -r 10

# Batch with local files mounted
docker run --rm -it -v "$PWD:/data" -w /data ghcr.io/amnottdevv/atdork:latest \
  --batch-file dorks.txt --format json -o out.json

# Persist the package store between runs
docker volume create atdork-store
docker run --rm -it -v atdork-store:/home/atdork/.atdork \
  ghcr.io/amnottdevv/atdork:latest install @cve/cve_1.txt

Full details in Docker.

docs.title: Anonymity & Proxies
docs.text:
# Route through Tor (requires the tor service running)
atdork -q "site:example.com" --tor

# Custom proxy
atdork -q "site:example.com" --proxy http://127.0.0.1:8080

# Refuse to fall back to your real IP if the proxy dies
atdork -q "site:example.com" --proxy http://127.0.0.1:8080 --ip-guard

See Proxy & Anonymity for rotation pools and anonymity levels.

docs.title: Package Subcommands
docs.text:
The built-in package manager treats Atdork-DB — 123 packages, 31 @folders, ~994,600 dorks — like a package registry. Browse packages in the web catalog or with atdork search / atdork index.

Subcommand Description atdork search <keyword> Filter the package index by keyword (ref, folder, description). atdork index List every package: ref \| dorks \| size \| description. atdork install <ref> Copy a package into the local store (~/.atdork/packages). atdork uninstall <ref> Remove an installed package. atdork installed List installed packages in the local store. atdork update git pull --ff-only on the Atdork-DB checkout.

Package refs accept several forms — see Dork Database for the full grammar:

atdork search shodan                # find packages
atdork install @cve/cve_1.txt       # canonical: folder + file
atdork install c@cve_1.txt          # shorthand (unique folder prefix)
atdork install @ghdb                # whole folder
atdork installed                    # verify the store
atdork update                       # refresh the database checkout

docs.title: Environment Subcommands
docs.text:
Manage isolated workspaces — every file AtDork writes stays inside the environment root. Full guide: Environment.

Subcommand Description atdork env create <path> [--name N] Create the workspace layout + marker (idempotent; init is an alias). atdork env list List registered environments. atdork env use <path> Set the default active environment. atdork env which Show the resolved environment and its owned paths. atdork env info Size per area, results count, DB clone status. atdork env destroy <path> [--delete] Unregister (keep files) or delete the folder. 
atdork env create ~/osint-job        # one-time
atdork env use ~/osint-job           # default for every command
atdork -q "inurl:admin"              # results land in <root>/results/
atdork --env /other/job -q "..."     # per-command override

Installed packages run as batch files (--batch-file c@cve_1.txt); any ref also loads directly from the database root via --database-dork (see below).

docs.title: Workflow Subcommands
docs.text:
Run sequential multi-step dork campaigns defined in YAML. Full guide: Workflows.

Subcommand Description atdork workflow list List available workflows (config workflows: + discovered files). atdork workflow validate [name] Validate definitions (schema, substitutions, targets). Exit 1 on errors. atdork workflow run <name> Run a workflow. <name> may also be a file path or . (the single workflow found in the root). Flag (on run) Description --file FILE Workflow YAML file(s), repeatable (also on list/validate). --target TARGET Override the workflow target ({target} substitution). --workers N Override the worker (thread) count for every step. --step NAME Run only this step. --resume Skip steps already completed in the saved state. --dry-run Print resolved queries without searching.

One-shot flags on the main command (same engine, no subcommand):

Flag Description --run-workflow NAME Run a workflow by name, file path, or . for the single workflow discovered in the root. --workflow-file FILE Read workflow definitions from this file. --workflow-target TARGET Override the workflow target. --workflow-workers N Override the worker (thread) count. --workflow-resume Resume: skip completed steps. --workflow-dry-run Print resolved queries without searching. 
atdork workflow list                     # what's defined?
atdork workflow validate                 # schema check, no credits spent
atdork --run-workflow .                  # run the single workflow in ./workflow.yaml
atdork workflow run recon-acme --target example.com --workers 2
atdork workflow run recon-acme --resume   # continue after a failed/stopped run

Workflow files named workflow.yaml (etc.) in the active environment root or the working directory are discovered automatically; the environment root wins on name collisions.

docs.title: Watch Subcommands
docs.text:
One-shot monitoring: register dorks, then report only the new findings each cycle. Full guide: Watch Mode.

Subcommand Description atdork watch add <name> Create (or extend) a watch: --dork, --batch-file, --database-dork, --notify. atdork watch list List watches with their source summary and last run. atdork watch show <name> Show the definition, options, history counters and last new URLs. atdork watch run <name> Run one cycle (cron-friendly). --all runs every watch. atdork watch remove <name> Delete the watch and its history. Flag (on add / run) Description --dork DORK Dork to run (repeatable on add). --batch-file FILE File of dorks, one per line (repeatable on add). --database-dork SPEC Database dork spec, e.g. @ghdb/01_footholds. --notify TARGET Webhook target (discord: / slack: / telegram:). Stored on add, overridable on run. --backend, --max-results, --timeout, --retries, --delay, --region, --safesearch, --timelimit Search options (stored on add, overridable on run). --dry-run (run) Resolve the dorks and exit — nothing searched. --concurrency N (run) Parallel dork workers (default 1). --all (run) Run every saved watch. 
atdork watch add acme --dork "site:acme.com ext:env" --notify discord:https://…
atdork watch run acme              # first run = baseline, later runs report the delta
atdork watch run acme --dry-run    # sanity-check the dorks, no credits spent
atdork watch run --all             # one cycle for every watch

State lives in <env>/state/watch/<name>.json; runs never use the search cache, and a quiet cycle (no new findings) sends no notification.

docs.title: Plugin Subcommands
docs.text:
Installable Python tools that surface as --<plugin>-<option> flags on the main command. Full guide: Plugins.

Subcommand Description atdork plugins list List discovered plugins with status (ready / disabled / invalid). atdork plugins info <name> Show a plugin's contract, flags, dests, and path. atdork plugins run <name> [--opt KEY=VALUE] Run a plugin without the flag syntax. atdork plugins publish <ref> Print Index.idn lines for a tool folder (--write updates the file). atdork plugins sources List third-party registries configured under plugins.sources. 
atdork install @plugins/dorkbuilder              # install a tool folder
atdork install https://github.com/user/repo#tool # or from a git repo
atdork install --source mine @plugins/tool       # or from your own registry
atdork --dorkbuilder-text "John wick" --dorkbuilder-save dorks.txt
atdork plugins run dorkbuilder --opt text=Acme --opt limit=3
atdork plugins publish @plugins/dorkbuilder --write

atdork install also accepts --git-ref BRANCH to pin a repository URL to a branch or tag, and --source NAME to install from a registry declared in plugins.sources.

Every option is registered as --<plugin>-<option> (the engine prefixes short option names itself). A plugin runs via the bare --<plugin> trigger or implicitly when any --<plugin>-* argument is present.

docs.title: Query & Results
docs.text: Flag Description -q, --query Main search query (dork). Can be combined with --batch-separator for multiple queries. -r, --max-results Maximum number of results to return per query. Values above 100 are automatically clamped. --batch-file Path to a text file containing one dork per line. Lines starting with # are ignored. --batch-separator Separator for splitting a single -q string into multiple queries. Default is ;.

docs.title: Output Options
docs.text: Flag Description -o, --output Save all results to a single file. Format determined by --format or file extension. --output-dir Save each query's results to a separate file in the specified directory. --format Output format: txt (human-readable), json (structured), csv (spreadsheet). -v, --verbose Display results in real-time during batch processing. --no-snippet Hide result snippets in terminal output for cleaner display.

docs.title: Templates
docs.text: Flag Description --template Load one or more YAML templates (comma-separated). Example: --template sqli,wordpress --target Domain to substitute for {target} placeholder in template dorks. --select Run only specific dorks from a template (1-based indices). Example: --select 1,3,5 --list-templates Display all available templates with descriptions. --template-path Custom directory to search for template files. --preview Show template dorks without executing them. Useful for validation.

docs.title: Search Engine Settings
docs.text: Flag Description --region Search region/language code. Examples: us-en, uk-en, de-de, ru-ru. --safesearch Filter adult content: on (strict), moderate (default), off (none). --timelimit Restrict results by time: d (day), w (week), m (month), y (year). --backend Search engine(s) to use. Options: google, bing, duckduckgo, startpage, yandex, auto, a comma-separated list — or an API engine configured under engines: in atdork.yml (serper, serpapi, brave) or a profiles: chain name. See Engines & Providers.

docs.title: Request Tuning
docs.text: Flag Description --user-agent Custom User-Agent string. If not provided, AtDork rotates through a built-in pool. --timeout Request timeout in seconds. Increases progressively with retries. --retries Number of retry attempts per backend before moving to the next. --delay Fixed delay between requests in seconds. Overridden by --adaptive-delay if enabled.

docs.title: Proxy & Anonymity
docs.text: Flag Description --proxy Comma-separated list of proxy URLs. Format: scheme://[user:pass@]host:port. --proxy-file Path to a file containing proxy URLs (one per line). Lines starting with # are ignored. --tor Enable Tor SOCKS5 proxy at socks5h://127.0.0.1:9050. --strict Fail closed – if all proxies fail, AtDork exits with error instead of falling back to direct connection. --proxy-cooldown Seconds to wait before retrying a failed proxy (default: 60). --max-failures Number of consecutive failures before a proxy is permanently removed (default: 3). --ip-guard Enable IP leak detection. Requires --strict. AtDork stops if your real IP is exposed.

docs.title: Concurrency & Resilience
docs.text: Flag Description --concurrency Number of parallel threads for batch processing (1-10). Higher values = faster but more likely to hit rate limits. --max-fallback-failures Consecutive failures before falling back from parallel to sequential mode. --resilient Enable intelligent fault-tolerance: circuit breaker, backend fallback, and automatic retry. --adaptive-delay Dynamically adjust request delay based on real-time backend response codes.

docs.title: Post-Processing
docs.text: Flag Description --exec Execute a shell command on each result URL. Use {} as placeholder for the URL. Example: --exec "curl -I {}" --exec-on-vuln Execute command only on results flagged as vulnerable by --filter-vuln. --exec-parallel Number of parallel processes for --exec commands. Default: 1. --exec-timeout Timeout in seconds for each --exec command. Default: 30.

docs.title: Validation & Filtering
docs.text: Flag Description --no-validate Disable all spam/invalid result filtering. Keeps raw results. --strict-filter Enable strict validation: title ≥ 5 chars, description ≥ 10 chars, spam detection on, URL all mode. --validate-url URL validation mode: only (domain only), path (domain+path), params (domain+params), all (full), false (disabled). --validate-title Minimum title length. Set to false to disable title validation. --validate-desc Minimum description length. Set to false to disable description validation. --validate-spam Enable/disable spam detection. Default: true. --filter-vuln Filter results by vulnerability platform. Examples: wordpress, joomla, sqli, wordpress-link.

docs.title: Database & History
docs.text: Flag Description --db-path Path to SQLite database file. Default: atdork.db. --resume Resume pending or failed queries from the database. --history Display search history with query text and status. --no-dedup Disable global URL deduplication. Keeps all results. --export-db Export entire database to JSON or CSV. Example: --export-db all_results.json

docs.title: Dork Database & Package Manager
docs.text:
Load dorks straight from the Atdork-DB checkout without installing them first. Full workflow and the package list: Dork Database.

Flag Description --database-dork SPEC Load dorks from database ref(s). Comma-separated, folder or file level. Example: --database-dork @ghdb/01_footholds,@lfi. --database-preview Show the loaded dorks without executing them. Requires --database-dork. --database-r N Randomly select N dorks from the loaded set before running. --database-seed N Seed the RNG used by --database-r for reproducible selection. --database-path PATH Custom database root directory (instead of the discovered checkout). --database-dork-extract PATH Extract a ref to PATH instead of running it (v1.3.9.5+). --list-database-dork List every dork file available in the database and exit. --db-repo PATH Point the package manager at a specific Atdork-DB checkout. Overrides discovery. --db-repo-url URL Git URL of the Atdork-DB repository (used by clone/update helpers). --package-dir PATH Local package store directory. Default: ~/.atdork/packages. 
atdork --list-database-dork                                   # what's available?
atdork --database-dork @cve --database-preview                # show, don't run
atdork --database-dork @ghdb/01_footholds -r 20               # run a file
atdork --database-dork @cms --database-r 50 --database-seed 7 # random 50, reproducible

docs.title: Logging & Debugging
docs.text: Flag Description --log-file Path to log file. Default: atdork.log. --debug Enable debug logging (more verbose output). --no-verify Disable SSL certificate verification (not recommended). --no-fallback-backends Disable automatic backend fallback on failure.

docs.title: Configuration & Mode
docs.text: Flag Description --config Path to YAML configuration file (schema v2). Files are layered global → working dir → --config (see Configuration); CLI flags override YAML values. Env alternative: ATDORK_CONFIG. --interactive Launch interactive mode with prompts instead of CLI flags. --version Display version and exit. -h, --help Display help message and exit.

docs.title: Configuration (atdork.yml)
docs.text:
AtDork can be configured with YAML files instead of long CLI flag chains. The loader understands schema v2: nested sections for search behaviour, API engines, profiles, resilience tuning and output — while every legacy flat key from schema v1 keeps working unchanged.

A ready-to-copy example lives at examples/atdork.yml.

docs.title: Where config files are read from
docs.text:
Discovery is layered — every file that exists is loaded and merged, lowest precedence first:

# Layer Location 1 Built-in defaults (compiled into AtDork) 2 Global file ~/.config/atdork/config.yml (or .yaml / atdork.yml / atdork.yaml — first match wins) 3 Working directory ./atdork.yaml or ./AtDork.yaml or ./atdork.yml (first match wins) 4 Explicit file --config path/to/atdork.yml (or env ATDORK_CONFIG when --config is absent) 5 Environment ATDORK_<KEY> variables (flat keys only) 6 CLI flags always win

A single --config file therefore overrides the CWD file, which overrides the global file, which overrides the defaults — for every key each layer sets.

atdork -q "inurl:admin" --config ./team-config.yml   # ./team-config.yml wins over all files
ATDORK_CONFIG=~/.config/atdork/config.yml atdork -q "test"

docs.title: Complete example
docs.text:
# atdork.yml — schema v2
version: 2

# ── Search behaviour ─────────────────────────────────────────────
search:
  max_results: 30              # 1–100
  region: "us-en"              # <country>-<language>
  safesearch: "moderate"       # on | moderate | off
  timelimit: null              # d | w | m | y | null
  backend: "auto"              # auto, google, serper, a profile name, ...
  fallback:                    # explicit fallback chain (see engines.md)
    - google
    - serper
    - brave
  timeout: 10
  retries: 2
  delay: 0.0
  concurrency: 4

# ── Third-party search APIs (see engines.md) ────────────────────
engines:
  serper:
    type: api
    api_key: ${SERPER_API_KEY} # resolved from the environment — never a literal
    qps: 1                     # local rate limit, requests per second (0 = off)
  serpapi:
    type: api
    api_key: ${SERPAPI_KEY}
    qps: 1
  brave:
    type: api
    api_key: ${BRAVE_API_KEY}
    qps: 1

# ── Named backend chains: --backend resilient ───────────────────
profiles:
  resilient: [google, serper, brave]
  cheap: [duckduckgo, mojeek]  # scraping only, no API credits

# ── Resilience tuning (used with --resilient) ───────────────────
resilience:
  circuit_breaker:
    failure_threshold: 5       # failures before the breaker opens (default 3)
    reset_timeout: 90          # seconds before the breaker tries again
  cooldown: 90                 # overrides reset_timeout if both are set

# ── Output ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────
output:
  format: json                 # txt | json | csv
  dir: ./results               # alias: output_dir
  no_snippet: false

docs.title: search:
docs.text:
Search knobs. Every key here overrides the same key written at the file root (legacy style) or the built-in default.

Key Type Default Description max_results int 20 Results per query (1–100). region str us-en <country>-<language> region code. safesearch str moderate on, moderate, off. timelimit str/null null d, w, m, y. backend str auto Backend, comma list, API engine, or profile name. fallback list/str (ddgs default chain) Explicit fallback order, e.g. [google, serper, brave]. Replaces the built-in chain; also feeds --resilient. timeout int 10 Per-attempt timeout (seconds). retries int 2 Retries per backend. delay float 0.0 Delay between requests (seconds). user_agent str/null null null = auto-rotate. proxy / proxy_file str/null null Proxy URL(s) or file. tor bool false Enable Tor fallback. strict bool false Fail instead of falling back to direct. proxy_cooldown int 60 Seconds before a banned proxy is retried. max_failures int 3 Consecutive failures before permanent proxy removal. concurrency int 1 Worker threads. batch_separator str ; Separator for inline multi-query strings. resilient bool false Same as --resilient. adaptive_delay bool false Same as --adaptive-delay. no_fallback_backends bool false Same as --no-fallback-backends.

docs.title: engines:
docs.text:
Third-party search APIs keyed by engine name. Full guide: Engines & Providers.

engines:
  serper:
    type: api                  # only supported type
    api_key: ${SERPER_API_KEY}
    qps: 1.0
    timeout: 10
    # provider-specific options: engine, gl, hl, location, country, ...

A configured name overrides a built-in scraping backend of the same name — engines.brave makes --backend brave use the official Brave Search API.

docs.title: profiles:
docs.text:
Named backend chains usable as --backend <name>:

profiles:
  resilient: [google, serper, brave]

atdork -q "inurl:admin" --backend resilient

A profile is an explicit choice, so it is honoured even with --no-fallback-backends. Entries may include API engines.

docs.title: resilience:
docs.text:
Applied when --resilient (or search.resilient: true) is active:

Key Default Description circuit_breaker.failure_threshold 3 Failures before the circuit opens. circuit_breaker.reset_timeout 120 Seconds before the breaker half-opens. cooldown (unset) Cooldown in seconds; overrides reset_timeout when both are set.

docs.title: output:
docs.text: Key Maps to Description format format txt, json, csv. dir / output_dir output_dir Default results directory. no_snippet no_snippet Hide snippets in terminal output.

docs.title: workflows
docs.text: Reserved for the workflow engine (sequential multi-step runs). Accepted and validated as a mapping, not yet executed.

docs.title: Environment variable interpolation
docs.text:
Any YAML string value may reference the environment:

engines:
  serper:
    api_key: ${SERPER_API_KEY}          # must be set, or config load fails
proxy: socks5://${PROXY_USER}:${PROXY_PASS}@10.0.0.1:9050
user_agent: ${USER_AGENT:-AtDork/1.4}   # ${VAR:-default} — default when unset

Rules:

  • ${VAR} — expanded from the environment. In engines.*.api_key an unset variable aborts startup with an exact error:
Config error: /home/you/atdork.yml: engines.serper.api_key: environment 'SERPER_API_KEY' is not set

In any other key an unset variable logs a warning and degrades to an empty string. - ${VAR:-default} — uses default when VAR is unset (never fails). - Interpolation happens per file, before merging layers.

API keys are never stored in plaintext in AtDork's docs or examples — always inject them via ${ENV}, and never commit a file containing real keys. Keys that do end up in config are masked in logs/repr (***cd34) and stripped from error messages by the redactor.

docs.title: Environment & CLI overrides
docs.text:
Flat (root/search) keys can be overridden with ATDORK_<KEY> — types are coerced automatically:

export ATDORK_MAX_RESULTS=50     # int
export ATDORK_DEBUG=true         # bool: true/1/yes
export ATDORK_BACKEND=serper     # str

Nested sections (engines, profiles, ...) are never replaced by env strings. CLI flags always beat the file:

atdork -q "test" --max-results 5 --backend google   # flags win over yml + env

docs.title: Legacy schema v1 files
docs.text:
Files without any v2 section and without version: keep the old behaviour:

# v1 — still fully supported
max_results: 50
region: "uk-en"
backend: "google"
format: "json"
  • Unknown keys are ignored (debug log), as in previous versions.
  • search:, output: etc. are simply absent; defaults apply.

docs.title: Migrating to v2
docs.text:
1. Add version: 2.
  2. Move search knobs under search: (optional — root keys still work).
  3. Move format/output_dir under output: (optional).
  4. Add engines:/profiles: as needed.
  5. Once version: 2 (or any section) is present, validation is strict: typos and unknown keys fail fast with the list of known keys.

docs.title: Validation & errors
docs.text:
Problem Behaviour Unknown key in a v2 file ConfigError listing known keys Unknown key inside search:/output: ConfigError listing known keys Wrong section type (e.g. profiles.x not a list) ConfigError with the exact path Unparseable YAML ConfigError: ... failed to parse YAML: ... Unsupported version: ConfigError (supported: 1, 2) engines.*.api_key → unset ${VAR} ConfigError naming file + path + variable Engine present but key empty at query time clear runtime error, engine skipped, fallback continues

Config errors abort startup with a non-zero exit code so a broken file never silently changes search behaviour.

docs.title: Security checklist
docs.text:
• Store keys in the environment (export SERPER_API_KEY=...), reference them with ${SERPER_API_KEY}.
  • Keep atdork.yml out of version control when it contains anything environment-specific, or keep values in ${VAR} form.
  • Logs and error messages pass through the redactor — API keys, URL credentials and bearer tokens are masked automatically.
  • ~/.config/atdork/config.yml is a good place for stable personal defaults; use --config for per-project/team overrides.

docs.title: Contributing to AtDork
docs.text: Thank you for considering a contribution. AtDork is an ethical OSINT tool – please make sure every change aligns with that principle.

docs.title: Getting Started
docs.text:
1. Fork the repository.
  2. Clone your fork locally.
  3. Create a new branch from main: 
    git checkout -b feature/your-feature
  4. Make your changes and test them thoroughly.

docs.title: Development Setup
docs.text:
pip install -r requirements.txt
pip install pytest   # for running tests

docs.title: Running Tests
docs.text:
All new code should be covered by tests.

pytest tests/ -v

docs.title: Pull Request Process
docs.text:
1. Ensure your branch is up to date with main.
  2. Run the full test suite and confirm nothing is broken.
  3. Write clear commit messages (one feature per commit).
  4. Open a pull request with a descriptive title and a summary of changes.
  5. Link any related issues (e.g., Closes #12).

A maintainer will review your PR. Small, focused pull requests are reviewed faster.

docs.title: Code Style
docs.text:
• Follow PEP 8 for Python code.
  • Use black for automatic formatting (line length 88 is fine).
  • Add docstrings to new public functions.
  • Keep modules focused – one responsibility per file.

docs.title: Ethical Standards
docs.text:
AtDork is designed for legal, authorised security testing only. When contributing:

  • Do not add features that encourage illegal activity or unauthorised access.
  • Do not include hardcoded credentials, malware, or spyware.
  • Respect user privacy and data protection laws.

Violations of these standards will result in immediate removal of contributions and may be reported.

docs.title: Questions?
docs.text: Open a discussion or email the maintainer.

docs.title: Docker
docs.text: Run AtDork in a container — no local Python required. The image bundles the CLI, its dependencies and a baked copy of the Atdork-DB dork database, and runs as a non-root user (atdork).

docs.title: Get the image
docs.text:
# published image (built & smoke-tested by CI on every push)
docker pull ghcr.io/amnottdevv/atdork:latest

# or build it from source
git clone https://github.com/amnottdevv/atdork.git
cd atdork
docker build -t atdork .

Version-pinned images are published for every release tag (ghcr.io/amnottdevv/atdork:1.4.1), plus latest on every push to master.

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text:
alias atdork='docker run --rm -it -v "$PWD":/work ghcr.io/amnottdevv/atdork:latest'

atdork --version
atdork search "exposed s3 bucket" --limit 10
atdork --batch-file dorks.txt -r 20

/work is the container's working directory — mount your current directory so input files (--batch-file, --output) and results are visible on the host.

docs.title: Dork database
docs.text:
The Atdork-DB checkout is baked into the image at /opt/atdork-db (selected via the ATDORK_DB_REPO environment variable). To keep installed packages and a fresh database between runs, add a named volume:

docker volume create atdork-data

docker run --rm -v atdork-data:/opt/atdork-db ghcr.io/amnottdevv/atdork:latest index
docker run --rm -v atdork-data:/opt/atdork-db ghcr.io/amnottdevv/atdork:latest install @cve/cve_1.txt
docker run --rm -v atdork-data:/opt/atdork-db ghcr.io/amnottdevv/atdork:latest installed

If the mounted directory is empty, the entrypoint clones the database automatically on first run. To use your own checkout instead:

docker run --rm -v "$HOME/Atdork-DB":/opt/atdork-db ghcr.io/amnottdevv/atdork:latest search cve

To refresh the baked database of a locally built image, just rebuild (docker build -t atdork .) — the clone step always fetches main.

docs.title: Environment variables
docs.text: Variable Default Purpose ATDORK_DB_REPO /opt/atdork-db Root of the Atdork-DB checkout the package manager reads ATDORK_DB_URL https://github.com/amnottdevv/Atdork-DB Repository cloned by the entrypoint when the database is missing

docs.title: Interactive shell inside the container
docs.text: docker run --rm -it --entrypoint sh ghcr.io/amnottdevv/atdork:latest

docs.title: GHDB scrape into a persistent store
docs.text:
docker run --rm -v "$PWD":/work -v atdork-data:/opt/atdork-db \
  ghcr.io/amnottdevv/atdork:latest --ghdb-scrape "exposed passwords" \
  --ghdb-after 2024-01-01 --output results.json

docs.title: docker compose
docs.text:
services:
  atdork:
    image: ghcr.io/amnottdevv/atdork:latest
    volumes:
      - ./work:/work
      - atdork-data:/opt/atdork-db
volumes:
  atdork-data:

docker compose run --rm atdork search cve --limit 5

docs.title: Image details
docs.text:
• Base: python:3.12-slim (Debian), CLI installed with pip install .
  • Runtime user: atdork (non-root, uid auto) — mount with matching permissions for files you need to write on the host
  • git is included so atdork update and the first-run database bootstrap work
  • CI (.github/workflows/docker-publish.yml) builds the image and runs smoke tests (--version, index, search, install/installed, fresh-volume bootstrap) before publishing to GHCR on every push and tag

docs.title: Engines & Providers
docs.text:
AtDork searches through two kinds of engines:

  1. Built-in scraping engines — provided by the ddgs library, no account needed (default behaviour).
  2. Third-party API providers — official paid/free search APIs (Serper.dev, SerpApi, Brave Search API), configured under engines: in atdork.yml. Deterministic results, higher reliability, but they consume your API credits.

Both kinds are selected the same way — with --backend, search.backend, or a profiles: chain — and both feed the identical downstream pipeline (validation, filtering, dedupe, cache, resume, output formats).

docs.title: Built-in engines (scraping)
docs.text:
Backend Notes auto Default: ddgs picks its best source per query. google Google via ddgs. bing Bing via ddgs. duckduckgo DuckDuckGo (first entry of the default fallback chain). brave Brave scraping backend — unless overridden by engines.brave (API). mojeek Mojeek — light scraping footprint. startpage Startpage. wikipedia Wikipedia (last default fallback). yandex, yahoo Available via ddgs.

The default fallback chain (when search.fallback is not configured) is:

duckduckgo → bing → brave → mojeek → startpage → wikipedia

atdork -q "inurl:admin"                    # auto
atdork -q "inurl:admin" --backend google   # force one scraping backend
atdork -q "test" --no-fallback-backends    # single backend only, no chain

No API key, no account, no config required.

docs.title: API providers
docs.text:
Add them under engines: in atdork.yml (see Configuration):

version: 2
engines:
  serper:
    type: api
    api_key: ${SERPER_API_KEY}
    qps: 1
  serpapi:
    type: api
    api_key: ${SERPAPI_KEY}
    qps: 1
  brave:
    type: api
    api_key: ${BRAVE_API_KEY}
    qps: 1

export SERPER_API_KEY=...     # or SERPAPI_KEY / BRAVE_API_KEY
atdork -q "site:github.com password" --backend serper

docs.title: Supported providers at a glance
docs.text:
Engine Endpoint Key env var Free tier* Per-request cap qps default serper POST google.serper.dev/search SERPER_API_KEY one-time credits (≈2,500) 100 1.0 serpapi GET serpapi.com/search SERPAPI_KEY 100 searches/month 100 1.0 brave GET api.search.brave.com/res/v1/web/search BRAVE_API_KEY 2,000 queries/month 20 1.0

* Free-tier figures are what the providers published last we checked — always confirm on their pricing pages. qps is AtDork's local limiter (minimum interval between your own requests); raise or lower it to match your plan (qps: 0 disables it).

docs.title: Parameter support matrix
docs.text:
How AtDork's common search parameters map per provider:

Parameter serper serpapi brave query + max_results ✅ q, num ✅ q, num ✅ q, count (max 20) region (us-en) ✅ gl/hl ✅ gl/hl ✅ country/search_lang safesearch ⚪ ignored ⚪ ignored (engine-dependent) ✅ safesearch off/moderate/strict timelimit (d/w/m/y) ⚪ ignored ✅ tbs=qdr:d… ✅ freshness=pd/pw/pm/py proxy + custom UA ✅ applied per request ✅ ✅

Provider-specific options can be passed through engines.<name> and land in the request (e.g. engine: google-news for serpapi, location: Paris, France for serper, offset: 20 for brave):

engines:
  serpapi:
    type: api
    api_key: ${SERPAPI_KEY}
    engine: google
    tbs: ""            # extra query params via options

docs.title: Result normalisation
docs.text: Every provider response is normalised to AtDork's internal shape — {title, href, body} — so filters, dedupe, cache, resume and all output formats behave identically to scraping results.

docs.title: Backend resolution & override rules
docs.text:
For every backend name AtDork tries, resolution order is:

  1. Registry — is the name configured under engines:? → use the API provider. A configured name overrides a built-in backend with the same name (engines.brave → Brave Search API instead of ddgs scraping).
  2. Otherwise → built-in ddgs scraping path.
# API directly
atdork -q "inurl:test" --backend serper

# explicit chain: scraping first, API last
atdork -q "inurl:test" --backend google,serper

# profile from atdork.yml
atdork -q "inurl:test" --backend resilient

docs.title: The fallback chain
docs.text:
search:
  backend: auto
  fallback: [google, serper, brave]   # or "google,serper,brave"

Behaviour:

Situation Queue backend: auto + chain configured auto first, then the chain single backend + chain that backend, then the chain comma list (google,serper) used as-is profile name profile list as-is (even with --no-fallback-backends) no chain configured built-in ddgs default chain

What happens on provider errors:

Error kind Detected from Behaviour quota (credits exhausted) HTTP 402/403, body keywords, serpapi error field provider skipped, next backend immediately, no retry rate_limit (429) HTTP 429 same as quota (treated as rate limit) auth (bad key) HTTP 401/403 skipped, clear log line config (key not set) empty api_key skipped; raised at the end if nothing was found network / parse / api timeouts, bad JSON, other 4xx/5xx retried on the same backend with backoff, then next

Credit caution: a provider in the chain is queried for every query that reaches it — including queries that legitimately have zero results (an empty scraper result advances to the next backend). If API credits are precious, either keep API engines out of fallback and invoke them explicitly with --backend serper, or make them the first entry so you pay only one API call per query instead of chain-tail calls after every empty scrape.

docs.title: Configuration reference for engines.<name>
docs.text: Key Default Description type api Only api is supported (validated at load). provider (name) Implementation when the key differs from the class name (e.g. two serper accounts: myserper: {provider: serper, ...}). api_key — ${ENV} interpolation strongly recommended; unset ${ENV} fails at load, empty value fails at query time with a clear error. qps 1.0 Local rate limit (requests/second, 0 = unlimited). Shared across worker threads. timeout 10 HTTP timeout in seconds. (extra) — Passed to the provider as a request option (engine, gl, hl, location, country, search_lang, offset, ...).

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
Symptom Cause / fix Config error: ... engines.serper.api_key: environment 'SERPER_API_KEY' is not set Export the variable, use ${SERPER_API_KEY:-}, or remove the engine. engines.serper.api_key is not set — export SERPER_API_KEY... at query time Engine configured with an empty/literal-empty key; set the key. API quota exceeded (rate limit): ... in logs Out of credits — AtDork moves to the next backend automatically. Check your provider dashboard. Rate limited: ... Provider throttling — lower qps, or let the chain continue. Authentication failed: ... Key invalid/rotated — regenerate and update the env var. unknown provider 'x' (supported: brave, serpapi, serper) provider: / engine name typo in engines:. Brave results stop at 20 Free-tier per-request cap (count ≤ 20); paginate via offset option or use another provider for larger max_results.

Keys never appear in logs: requests/responses are passed through the redactor (api_key=***, ***last4, masked URL credentials), so it is safe to run with --debug when diagnosing provider issues.

docs.title: Installation Guide
docs.text:
AtDork requires Python >= 3.9 and works seamlessly across Linux (including WSL), macOS, and Windows — or no Python at all via Docker.

No local install? Use Docker

The official image ships the CLI plus the full dork database:

docker pull ghcr.io/amnottdevv/atdork:latest
docker run --rm -it ghcr.io/amnottdevv/atdork:latest -q "site:gov filetype:pdf"

Full details — volumes, networking, compose — in Docker.

docs.title: 1. Installation via PyPI (Recommended)
docs.text:
The most direct and stable method to acquire AtDork is via the Python Package Index:

pip install atdork

docs.title: 2. Installing From Source (Development Mode)
docs.text:
If you wish to test bleeding-edge features, inspect the code, or modify internal wordlists, build it locally:

# Clone the repository
git clone https://github.com/amnottdevv/atdork.git
cd atdork

# Install using editable mode
pip install -e .

docs.title: 3. One-Time Data Setup — Clone Atdork-DB
docs.text:
Since v1.3.9.7 AtDork ships code only; the dork packages (~994,600 dorks across 31 @folders) live in the Atdork-DB repository. The package manager (atdork search, atdork install, --database-dork) reads a local checkout. Clone it once:

git clone https://github.com/amnottdevv/Atdork-DB.git ~/Atdork-DB

AtDork discovers the checkout automatically in this order:

Priority Source Example 1 --db-repo flag (per command) atdork search cve --db-repo /opt/Atdork-DB 2 Environment variable export ATDORK_DB_REPO=~/Atdork-DB 3 Config file (db_repo) written by --db-repo + --write 4 ~/Atdork-DB default home checkout 5 Sibling of the AtDork checkout ../Atdork-DB 6 ./Atdork-DB current working directory

Docker users can skip this entirely — the image bundles the database at /opt/atdork-db (see Docker).

docs.title: 4. Post-Installation Verification
docs.text:
Validate that the CLI entry point successfully mapped to your system's PATH variables:

atdork --version

Expected output:

atdork 1.4.1

Verify the database connection as well:

atdork index          # lists all 123 packages (ref | dorks | size | description)
atdork search cve     # filters that list by keyword
atdork installed      # lists packages copied into your local store (~/.atdork/packages)

docs.title: 5. Optional Dependencies
docs.text:
If you plan to utilize Tor Integration, ensure the tor service is installed and running on your system before using the --tor flag.

sudo apt install tor     # Debian/Ubuntu
sudo systemctl start tor

docs.title: 6. Upgrading
docs.text:
pip install --upgrade atdork      # upgrade the CLI
atdork update                     # git pull the Atdork-DB checkout (refresh dorks)

docs.title: Quick Start Guide
docs.text: Get up and running with AtDork in less than a minute. These fundamental workflows illustrate how to structure passive target reconnaissance.

docs.title: 1. Execute a Standard Search Query
docs.text:
Discover exposed PDF archives hosted on public government domains. By default, AtDork targets 20 maximum entries using the optimal available engine backend.

atdork -q "site:gov filetype:pdf" -r 10

docs.title: 2. Storing Extracted Data to Disk
docs.text:
Save search index outputs straight to a cleanly parsed JSON payload file for upstream analysis:

atdork -q "intitle:index.of mp3" -r 20 --format json -o music.json

docs.title: 3. High-Throughput Batch Processing
docs.text:
Execute dozens of complex dorking patterns simultaneously.

  1. Create a plain text payload containing one dork profile per line, named dorks.txt:
site:edu filetype:xls
inurl:admin login
intitle:"index of" "backup"
  1. Pass the text map straight into the batch engine:
atdork --batch-file dorks.txt -r 20

docs.title: 4. Use the Dork Database (Packages)
docs.text:
AtDork ships code only — the ~994,600 dorks live in Atdork-DB, managed like a package registry. Browse the web catalog to explore packages, then install and run them:

# One-time: clone the data repo (skip if you use Docker — the image bundles it)
git clone https://github.com/amnottdevv/Atdork-DB.git ~/Atdork-DB

atdork search cve                # find packages by keyword
atdork install @cve/cve_1.txt    # install a package into ~/.atdork/packages
atdork --batch-file c@cve_1.txt -r 20   # run the installed package

atdork --database-dork @ghdb/01_footholds --database-preview   # show, don't run
atdork --database-dork @lfi -r 20                              # random sample run

docs.title: Operational Troubleshooting Manual
docs.text: Resolution protocols for common failure vectors encountered during large-scale network scanning sweeps.

docs.title: 1. Engine Backend Returning HTTP Code 429 (Rate-Limited)
docs.text:
• Symptom: Logs emit repetitive 429 Too Many Requests notifications, and result vectors drop to zero.
  • Mitigation Actions:
    • Increase your standard processing delay footprint: --delay 4.
    • Inject dynamic spacing algorithms into the engine loop: --adaptive-delay.
    • Deploy an expansive distribution pool of network targets: --proxy-file proxies.txt.
    • Shift target focus over to alternative data indexing platforms: --backend startpage or --backend yandex.

docs.title: 2. Proxies Falling Out of Pool Sync
docs.text:
• Symptom: Runtime outputs show extensive proxy failures, or execution hangs inside connection timeouts.
  • Mitigation Actions:
    • Verify proxy routing string schema declaration definitions. Format must strictly align to: scheme://user:pass@host:port.
    • Ensure that you deploy SOCKS5h variants (socks5h://) when leveraging Tor networks to force DNS lookups down the remote proxy pipeline rather than parsing local leak nodes.

docs.title: 3. CSV Output Rendering Corrupt or Displaying Security Warnings
docs.text:
• Symptom: Spreadsheet processors (Microsoft Excel, LibreOffice Calc) display warning flags regarding executable expressions or broken formatting blocks upon opening exported maps.
  • Mitigation Actions:
    • Update to the latest release: pip install --upgrade atdork (current: 1.4.1).
    • Distribution builds since 1.3.8 incorporate a parsing pass (lib/storage.py) that strips or prefixes symbols (+, =, -, @) to block Formula Injection attacks.

docs.title: 4. "Atdork-DB repository not found"
docs.text:
• Symptom: atdork search, atdork install, or --database-dork exits with Atdork-DB repository not found. Looked in: ...
  • Cause: The dork database is a separate checkout that hasn't been cloned (or discovered) yet.
  • Mitigation Actions:
    • Clone it once: git clone https://github.com/amnottdevv/Atdork-DB.git ~/Atdork-DB
    • Or point AtDork at an existing checkout: --db-repo /path/to/Atdork-DB or export ATDORK_DB_REPO=/path/to/Atdork-DB.
    • Docker users: the image bundles the database at /opt/atdork-db — this error should never occur; if it does, you overrode ATDORK_DB_REPO with a bad path.

docs.title:
5. "No package matches ''" or Ambiguous Shorthand
  • Symptom: install/uninstall fails with No package matches ... (optionally with a Did you mean: line), or Ambiguous shorthand.
  • Mitigation Actions:
    • Find the exact ref: atdork search <keyword> or browse the web catalog.
    • Use the canonical form @folder/file.txt when a shorthand prefix matches several folders.
    • Stale refs after manual DB edits? Rebuild the manifest inside the checkout: atdork index --build.

6. Stale Dork Data
  • Symptom: New folders or files (e.g. fresh GHDB sync) don't show up in atdork search / atdork index.
  • Mitigation Actions:
    • Refresh the checkout: atdork update (a git pull --ff-only on Atdork-DB).
    • Verify you're reading the checkout you think: the discovery order is --db-repo → ATDORK_DB_REPO → config db_repo → ~/Atdork-DB → sibling → ./Atdork-DB.

7. Docker: Installed Packages Don't Persist
  • Symptom: atdork install ... succeeds, but the next docker run shows an empty atdork installed.
  • Cause: The container filesystem is ephemeral — each docker run starts fresh.
  • Mitigation Actions:
    • Mount a volume over the store: -v atdork-store:/home/atdork/.atdork.
    • Or skip the store entirely and run refs straight from the bundled database: --database-dork @cve (works without install).

See Docker for volumes, bind mounts, and compose examples.

8. Environment: "… is not an AtDork environment" or "outside the environment"
  • Symptom: --env/ATDORK_ENV fails with missing .atdork-env, or a path is rejected with resolves to '…' which is outside the environment.
  • Mitigation Actions:
    • Create the workspace first: atdork env create <path> — an environment is a plain folder with a marker, not any directory.
    • While an environment is active all writes must stay inside its root; relative paths already resolve against the root (results/x.json → <root>/results/x.json), so prefer those.
    • Output still appearing in ./results/? No environment is actually active — verify with atdork env which.
    • Full guide: Environment.

9. Workflow: "'' not found" or Validation Errors
  • Symptom: atdork workflow run <name> / --run-workflow exits with Workflow '…' not found, or workflow validate prints schema errors.
  • Cause: The definition isn't in the merged sources (config workflows: + discovered files), or it violates the schema.
  • Mitigation Actions:
    • List what AtDork actually sees: atdork workflow list (each entry shows its source — config or file path).
    • Discovery looks for workflow.yaml / workflows.yaml (etc.) in the active environment root and the current directory only — not in parent folders. atdork env which tells you which root is active.
    • Fix schema errors with atdork workflow validate — errors are prefixed with the exact path (workflows.<name>.steps[2]: …) and exit non-zero (CI-friendly).
    • {target} errors mean a query uses the token but neither the workflow nor --target provides one.
    • Full reference: Workflows.

10. Workflow: Step "below_threshold" / "failed" / Resuming
  • Symptom: A step reports below_threshold, or the run stops with failed … (on_error: stop) and remaining steps never ran.
  • Cause: below_threshold simply means fewer unique results than when_results_below after the retry_with queries merged (often normal for small targets). failed means every query of that step errored out (backends exhausted).
  • Mitigation Actions:
    • Preview the exact queries first: --dry-run (or --workflow-dry-run) — no searches, no credits.
    • Inspect the step's retry_with list — alternate, broader dorks are the intended fix for thin results.
    • After fixing the definition (or after a rate-limit cooldown), continue where the run stopped: atdork workflow run <name> --resume — completed steps are skipped under the same run_id.
    • Force a single step in isolation: --step <name>.
    • State lives in <env>/state/workflows/<name>.json (or ~/.atdork/state/workflows/ without an environment) — delete it for a truly fresh start.

11. Plugin: Flag "unrecognized arguments" or Plugin Won't Run
  • Symptom: atdork --dorkbuilder-... exits with unrecognized arguments, or a plugin listed by plugins list doesn't fire.
  • Cause: The plugin isn't installed in the active package store (each environment has its own store), it's disabled in config, or its PLUGIN metadata is invalid.
  • Mitigation Actions:
    • List what the current environment actually sees: atdork plugins list — ready means the flags are registered.
    • Install into the active store: atdork install @plugins/<tool> (use atdork env which to confirm which store is active).
    • Check you're using the mandatory format --<plugin>-<option> — a fully spelled flag with the wrong prefix is rejected at registration.
    • An invalid entry prints the exact contract error (bad name, wrong option prefix, missing run()); fix the .py and reinstall.
    • Config defaults alone (plugins.options) never launch a plugin — a real --<plugin> or --<plugin>-* argument is required.
    • Full reference: Plugins.

12. Plugin: Installing From a URL, Git Repo or Custom Source Fails
  • Symptom: git is required to install from a repository URL …, contains N plugins; pick one with '#<subpath>', checksum mismatch … refusing to install, or unknown plugin source '<name>'.
  • Cause: Missing git binary, an ambiguous repo layout, a registry whose files drifted from its Index.idn, or a source that isn't declared in the active config layer.
  • Mitigation Actions:
    • Install git (apt install git / brew install git) — a single .py URL needs no git, repository installs do.
    • Point at one tool inside a multi-plugin repo: atdork install https://github.com/user/repo#my-tool.
    • A checksum mismatch means the registry index and its files disagree — re-run atdork plugins publish @plugins/<tool> --repo . --write in that registry, push it, then retry.
    • Check what the active layer sees with atdork plugins sources; --env uses the environment's config (<env>/.config/config.yml), not the working-directory file.
    • Share a registry safely by pinning it to a tag: ref: v1.2.0 under plugins.sources, or --git-ref v1.2.0 for a URL install.
    • Full reference: Plugins.

13. Plugin: Execution Error or Output Rejected by Environment Guard
  • Symptom: Plugin error: …, Plugin '<name>' crashed: …, or output escapes the environment root.
  • Cause: The plugin raised an exception, returned a non-integer, or tried to write a path outside the active environment root.
  • Mitigation Actions:
    • Run it directly for the full traceback: atdork plugins run <name> --opt k=v, or add --debug.
    • A run() must return an int exit code (None counts as 0) — a string/bool return is a contract violation.
    • The environment guard forces every write under the root — use ctx.guard_write() and a relative path (results/report.html), or run without --env.
    • Silence a misbehaving plugin without uninstalling: add it to plugins.disabled in config.

14. Watch: Nothing New, Wrong Findings, or No Notification
  • Symptom: watch run always reports 0 new, every result is reported as new on every run, or the webhook never fires.
  • Cause: The first run is a baseline by design; a changed dork target re-keys results; and quiet cycles (nothing new) never notify.
  • Mitigation Actions:
    • The very first watch run <name> records a baseline and reports nothing as new — that is expected. Run it twice to see the delta.
    • Every run without new findings stays quiet (no notification). Only the baseline and real findings notify.
    • Check what the watch holds: atdork watch show <name> lists the dorks, stored options, run counter and the last new URLs.
    • Verify the dorks resolve before spending time/credits: atdork watch run <name> --dry-run.
    • A different backend can return a different result set (so URLs may look "new"); pin the search options on add (--max-results, --region, --backend) so cycles are comparable.
    • Reset the history by deleting <env>/state/watch/<name>.json (or watch remove + watch add) — the next run becomes a fresh baseline.
    • Confirm the watch state file is the one you think it is: environments keep their own (atdork --env <path> watch list).
    • Full guide: Watch Mode.
Dork Database (Atdork-DB)
docs.text:
AtDork ships code only — the dork data lives in the separate Atdork-DB repository, which the built-in package manager treats like a package registry.

Packages 123 dork files Folders 31 themed @folders Dorks 994,603 unique queries Refresh GHDB re-synced weekly by CI

docs.title: 🔎 Browse the web catalog
docs.text:
→ https://amnottdevv.github.io/Atdork-DB/

The web catalog is the visual index of everything below:

docs.title: Bing & DuckDuckGo Dorks (@bing/, @duckduckgo/)
docs.text:
Data location: these dorks live in the Atdork-DB repository under @folders. Browse @bing / @duckduckgo in the web catalog → — search with atdork search bing, install with atdork install @bing/bing1.txt.

Bing and DuckDuckGo support several search operators that Google doesn't (or supports differently). This page covers what's unique about each engine and how the dork files use those operators.

Atdork-DB/
├── @bing/
│   ├── bing1.txt   # OR groups & contains:
│   └── bing2.txt   # location:, ip:, domain:, linkfromdomain:, language:, feed:, prefer:
└── @duckduckgo/
    ├── ddg1.txt     # Verbatim error strings, !bang shortcuts, OR combos
    └── ddgo.txt     # Parameter-style queries (cart, id, login params)

Run these with --backend bing or --backend duckduckgo so AtDork sends the query to the right engine:

atdork --database-dork @bing/bing1 --backend bing -r 20
atdork --database-dork @duckduckgo/ddg1 --backend duckduckgo -r 20

docs.title: Bing vs DuckDuckGo at a glance
docs.text: Aspect Bing DuckDuckGo Unique operators contains:, loc:/location:, ip:, domain:, linkfromdomain:, language:, feed:, prefer: !bang (14,000+ shortcuts), \ (jump to first result), !doodles, !safeoff OR grouping Full support with (), e.g. inurl:(A OR B) No () grouping — use plain OR or " " File search contains: — pages that link to a file type filetype: — same as Google Location filter loc:Indonesia Not available — use site:.id instead IP search ip:8.8.8.8 — all sites on that host Not available Tracking Standard No tracking by default

docs.title: 1. Bing — exclusive operators
docs.text: Operator Purpose Example contains: Find pages that link to a given file type contains:sql site:.id loc: / location: Filter by geographic location location:Indonesia inurl:?id= ip: Find every site hosted on one IP (shared hosting) ip:103.8.12.100 domain: Domain match, more precise than site: domain:go.id linkfromdomain: Pages linked from a given domain linkfromdomain:target.com inurl:admin language: Filter by content language language:indonesian inurl:?q= feed: Find RSS/Atom feeds feed:target.com prefer: Boost weight of a keyword prefer:mysql inurl:?id= inurl:(A OR B) Grouped OR inurl:(?id= OR ?page=)

docs.title: Bug Bounty Program Discovery Dorks (@bug-bounty/)
docs.text:
Data location: these dorks live in the Atdork-DB repository under @folders. Browse @bug-bounty in the web catalog → — search with atdork search bug-bounty, install with atdork install @bug-bounty/bbdorks.txt.

This category is different from the vulnerability-class dorks elsewhere in the database. Instead of finding a weak parameter, these dorks find organizations that run a bug bounty or responsible disclosure program — useful when you're looking for legitimate, in-scope targets to test against rather than testing at random.

@bug-bounty/
├── bbdorks.txt                     # Responsible disclosure pages, security.txt, VDP/bounty listings (69)
└── bug-bounty-dorks-sushiwushi.txt # Additional program & disclosure discovery dorks                  (36)

docs.title: What this category looks for
docs.text: Aspect Description Purpose Surfaces a company's published security contact, responsible disclosure policy, security.txt file, or bounty/reward program page — the legitimate starting point for any engagement. Common patterns inurl:security.txt, inurl:/responsible-disclosure/, inurl:/.well-known/security.txt, "vulnerability disclosure policy", "powered by hackerone", "powered by bugcrowd", "powered by synack". Region filters Several entries use site:*.*.nl, site:*.*.uk, site:*.*.de, etc. to find disclosure programs in a specific country's domains. r=h: syntax The r=h:nl / r=h:uk / r=h:eu suffixes are DuckDuckGo's region-restriction shorthand, equivalent to filtering results by country.

inurl:/responsible-disclosure/

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
# Install this collection (refs also work straight from Atdork-DB)
atdork install @bug-bounty

# Load and run the bug bounty discovery dorks
atdork --database-dork @bug-bounty/bbdorks -r 30

# Preview what would run, without executing
atdork --database-dork @bug-bounty/bbdorks --database-preview

# Random sample, reproducible with a seed
atdork --database-dork @bug-bounty/bbdorks --database-r 20 --database-seed 5

# Save discovered program pages to a file for later review
atdork --database-dork @bug-bounty/bbdorks -r 50 --format json -o programs.json

Since this category is mostly site:-restricted or region-restricted plain-text/intext: searches rather than inurl: parameter probes, it tends to work well on any backend — but DuckDuckGo (--backend duckduckgo) handles the r=h: region shorthand entries natively:

atdork --database-dork @bug-bounty/bbdorks --backend duckduckgo -r 30

docs.title: What to do with the results
docs.text:
A hit here just means the organization has a disclosure/bounty program — it's not permission to test anything you find. Before touching the target:

  1. Open the disclosure page and read the scope — many programs explicitly exclude certain subdomains, endpoints, or third-party services.
  2. Check whether they run through a platform (HackerOne, Bugcrowd, Synack, Intigriti) — if so, register there and follow their intake process rather than reporting directly.
  3. Confirm the rules of engagement (rate limits, no automated scanning, no social engineering, etc.) before running any of the other dork categories against that domain.

docs.title: ⚠️ Disclaimer & Legal Notice
docs.text:
Finding a company's disclosure page is legal and encouraged — that's the point of publishing one. The disclaimer below applies to what you do after finding a program, i.e. any testing against the target itself:

  1. Only test within the published scope of the program you found.
  2. Follow the program's stated rules of engagement and reporting process.
  3. For any target without a public program, get explicit written authorization before testing.

docs.title: Censys Search Dorks (@censys/censysdork.txt)
docs.text:
Data location: these dorks live in the Atdork-DB repository under @folders. Browse @censys in the web catalog → — search with atdork search censys, install with atdork install @censys/censysdork.txt.

Unlike the Google/Bing/DuckDuckGo dorks elsewhere in this database, Censys queries search a database of internet-wide scan results — banners, TLS certificates, JARM fingerprints, and service metadata collected by actually connecting to hosts. That makes this category fundamentally about asset and infrastructure discovery, not web-app parameter fuzzing, and it spans three very different use cases that deserve different handling:

@censys/
└── censysdork.txt
  1. Malware/C2 threat-intelligence hunting — finding malicious infrastructure (Cobalt Strike, Sliver, various RATs) so defenders can track, block, or report it. This is a defensive use case by nature.
  2. Industrial Control Systems (ICS/OT) discovery — finding internet-exposed physical infrastructure (power meters, gas pump controllers, wind turbines, EV chargers). This carries real-world physical-safety implications that web app testing doesn't.
  3. Misconfigured cloud services & dashboards — exposed Redis, Kubernetes, admin dashboards. Same authorized-testing rules as the rest of this database apply here.

docs.title: 1. Malware & C2 Infrastructure Hunting (threat intelligence)
docs.text:
These fingerprints (TLS certificate hashes, JARM fingerprints, HTTP body hashes) identify known command-and-control frameworks and malware panels. Security teams use these to find and report active malicious infrastructure — this is standard threat-intel/blue-team tradecraft, the same way antivirus vendors fingerprint malware samples.

# Cobalt Strike team servers
services.tls.certificates.leaf_data.issuer.common_name: "Major Cobalt Strike"

# Metasploit servers
services.http.response.html_title: "Metasploit" and
services.tls.certificates.leaf_data.subject.organization: "Rapid7"

# Sliver C2
services.jarm.fingerprint: "3fd21b20d00000021c43d21b21b43d41226dd5dfc615dd4a96265559485910"

# Unauthenticated open directories serving known offensive-tool filenames
same_service(
    services.http.response.html_title: "Index of /"
    and services.http.response.body: /.*?(cobaltstrike|sliver|mimikatz|rclone)\.(exe|ps1|bin).*/
)

atdork --database-dork @censys/censysdork --backend censys -r 20

What to do with a hit: report it. Censys and most JARM/certificate fingerprints exist specifically so defenders can identify and take down malicious infrastructure or feed it into blocklists — that's the intended downstream action, not connecting to or interacting with the server yourself.

docs.title: 2. Industrial Control Systems / OT Discovery
docs.text:
Read this section before running anything in this category.

Unlike a website with an LFI bug, the systems these queries find are often physical infrastructure: gas station fuel tank monitors, electric vehicle chargers, wind turbine controllers, power meters. A few things make this category categorically different from the rest of this database:

  • Interacting with these devices can cause real-world physical effects — industrial protocols (Modbus, S7, BACnet, etc.) were mostly designed assuming a trusted network and often have no authentication at all. Sending even a "read" command to a fragile or legacy OT device can crash it or trigger unintended behavior.
  • Discovery is not authorization. Finding that a device is reachable tells you nothing about who owns it or whether you have any right to touch it. There is no equivalent here to "it's my own test site" — you almost certainly do not know whose gas pump or turbine this is.
  • This is the domain of ICS-CERT / CISA advisories, not casual pentesting. If you're doing authorized OT security work, it's a specialized discipline with its own safety protocols (usually requiring coordination with the asset owner and often physical presence or a lab-replica environment before touching a live control system).

The responsible use of ICS-discovery queries is awareness and reporting — e.g. identifying that a critical system is unexpectedly internet-facing so it can be reported to the owner or a national CERT — not connecting to or issuing commands against it.

# Generic ICS protocol discovery
services.service_name: {BACNET, CODESYS, EIP, FINS, FOX, IEC60870_5_104, S7, MODBUS}

# Add this to exclude honeypots (hosts with 100+ services)
services.truncated: false

# Discovery only — do not follow up by connecting to anything found
atdork --database-dork @censys/censysdork --backend censys --database-preview

If you find an exposed ICS/OT device that looks like real critical infrastructure (utilities, transportation, medical, industrial), the appropriate action is reporting it to CISA's ICS reporting channel (or your country's equivalent CERT), not further probing.

docs.title: 3. Misconfigured Cloud Services & Dashboards
docs.text:
This part follows the same rules as the CMS Dorks and Common Dorks categories — authorized testing only, confirm and report, don't exploit further.

# Unauthenticated Redis
services.redis.ping_response: "PONG"

# Misconfigured Kubernetes
services.kubernetes.pod_names: *

# Exposed dashboards
services.http.response.html_title: "Welcome to ntopng"
same_service(services.http.request.uri: "*/dashboard/" and services.http.response.html_title: "Traefik")

atdork --database-dork @censys/censysdork --backend censys -r 20 --filter-vuln exposed-service

docs.text:

  1. Security testing on infrastructure you own.
  2. Official Bug Bounty programs with explicit written authorization from the target owner.
  3. Threat-intelligence research (identifying malicious infrastructure) intended for reporting/blocklisting, not interaction.
  4. Reporting exposed critical infrastructure to the responsible owner or a national CERT.

Strictly prohibited: connecting to, sending commands to, or otherwise interacting with any industrial control system, OT device, or piece of critical infrastructure without explicit authorization from its owner — regardless of whether it appears unauthenticated. docs.title: CMS-Specific Dorks (@cms/)
docs.text:
Data location: these dorks live in the Atdork-DB repository under @folders. Browse @cms in the web catalog → — search with atdork search cms, install with atdork install @cms/joomla.txt.

Where the common/ category targets generic parameter patterns across any PHP app, this category targets fingerprints specific to a given CMS/framework — file paths, default config locations, and version markers unique to Joomla, WordPress, Magento, and Laravel. This makes the dorks far more precise: a hit tells you not just "a parameter exists" but "this specific CMS is running here, at this version or plugin."

@cms/
├── joomla.txt      # Joomla components, admin paths, config exposure      (382)
├── wp.txt          # WP core paths, plugins, themes, wp-config exposure  (26,324)
├── wp2.txt         # Additional WordPress dorks (plugins & params)          (474)
├── magento.txt     # Magento admin, API, and config endpoints                (76)
└── laravel.txt     # Laravel .env exposure, debug mode, artisan routes      (422)

docs.title: 1. Joomla (joomla.txt)
docs.text:
Aspect Description Purpose Finds Joomla installations and their component/admin structure — many older third-party Joomla components (com_*) shipped with LFI or config-exposure bugs, so identifying the component footprint is the first step. Common patterns inurl:"/component/users/", inurl:administrator/index.php, intitle:"Joomla - Web Installer", mosConfig_absolute_path=, inurl:com_content. 
inurl:administrator/index.php intitle:"Joomla"
intitle:"Joomla - Web Installer"
inurl:index.php?option=com_content
inurl:index.php?option=com_users&view=login
site:target.com inurl:/administrator/
inurl:configuration.php~ site:target.com

atdork --database-dork @cms/joomla -r 20

docs.title: 2. WordPress (wp.txt)
docs.text:
Aspect Description Purpose Fingerprints WordPress core, active plugins/themes, and common misconfigurations (exposed wp-config.php backups, open registration, debug logs). Common patterns inurl:wp-content/plugins/, inurl:wp-login.php, intext:"Powered by WordPress", filetype:log inurl:wp-content/debug.log, wp-config.php.bak. 
inurl:/wp-content/plugins/ site:target.com
inurl:wp-login.php
intitle:"WordPress" intext:"Just another WordPress site"
filetype:log inurl:"wp-content/debug.log"
inurl:wp-config.php.bak OR inurl:wp-config.php.save
inurl:xmlrpc.php "Invalid method"

atdork --database-dork @cms/wp -r 20 --filter-vuln wordpress

docs.title: 3. Magento (magento.txt)
docs.text:
Aspect Description Purpose Finds Magento admin panels, REST/SOAP API endpoints, and exposed configuration — Magento stores are high-value targets because they process payment data, so admin-path and API exposure matters more than on a typical CMS. Common patterns inurl:/admin/ + intitle:"Magento Admin", inurl:/downloader/index.php, inurl:app/etc/local.xml, inurl:/index.php/admin/, inurl:/rest/V1/ (REST API root). 
intitle:"Magento Admin" inurl:/admin
inurl:app/etc/local.xml
inurl:/downloader/index.php
inurl:/index.php/admin/dashboard
inurl:/rest/V1/products site:target.com
inurl:var/log/system.log site:target.com

atdork --database-dork @cms/magento -r 20

docs.title: 4. Laravel (laravel.txt)
docs.text:
Aspect Description Purpose Laravel apps are dorked differently from the others — the framework itself is fairly secure by default, so the interesting cases are almost always misconfiguration: APP_DEBUG=true left on in production (which dumps stack traces with DB credentials), or a .env file directly accessible. Common patterns inurl:.env "APP_KEY=", intext:"Whoops, looks like something went wrong" (debug page), inurl:/storage/logs/laravel.log, inurl:/artisan. 
inurl:.env "APP_KEY=" "DB_PASSWORD="
intext:"Whoops, looks like something went wrong"
inurl:/storage/logs/laravel.log
inurl:"/telescope" intitle:"Telescope"
inurl:.env site:target.com filetype:env

atdork --database-dork @cms/laravel -r 20 --filter-vuln laravel

A live, readable .env file is the single most damaging Laravel misconfiguration you'll find this way — it typically contains the app key, DB credentials, mail credentials, and third-party API keys all in one file. Treat a hit here the same way you'd treat any other exposed-secret finding: don't use the credentials, report through the program's disclosure channel. See GitHub Secret-Exposure Dorks for the same guidance applied to code-hosting leaks.

docs.title: Combining across CMS categories
docs.text:
# Fingerprint all four CMS types against a scoped target in one batch
atdork --database-dork @cms/joomla,@cms/wp,@cms/magento,@cms/laravel \
  -r 40 --format json -o cms_recon.json
