docs.title: Plugins
docs.text:
Plugins extend AtDork with new commands without touching the core: a plugin is a single Python file that declares a PLUGIN metadata dictionary and a run() entry point. Installed through the package manager, every plugin option surfaces on the main CLI using the mandatory --<plugin>-<option> flag format, so plugin flags can never collide with core flags or with each other.

atdork install @plugins/dorkbuilder
atdork --dorkbuilder-text "John wick" \
       --dorkbuilder-type social-media \
       --dorkbuilder-save dorks.txt

▶ plugin dorkbuilder (~/.atdork/packages/plugins/dorkbuilder/dorkbuilder.py)
10 dork(s) for "John wick" [category: social-media]
  • site:linkedin.com/in "John wick"
  • site:twitter.com "John wick" OR site:x.com "John wick"
  ...
✔ saved 10 dorks → dorks.txt

docs.title: The plugin contract
docs.text:
A plugin is a .py file with one top-level PLUGIN literal dictionary and a run(args, ctx) function:

PLUGIN = {
    "name": "dorkbuilder",              # becomes the --dorkbuilder trigger
    "version": "1.0.0",
    "description": "Build ready-to-run dork lists from text + a category",
    "options": [
        {"name": "text", "help": "Text to hunt for"},
        {"name": "type", "choices": ["social-media", "all"],
         "default": "social-media"},
        {"name": "limit", "type": "int", "default": 0},
        {"name": "list-types", "action": "store_true"},
    ],
}

def run(args, ctx) -> int:
    text = args.dorkbuilder_text        # dest: <plugin>_<option>
    return 0

docs.title: Mandatory flag format
docs.text: Option names are declared in short form ("text"); the engine always registers them as --<plugin>-<option> (--dorkbuilder-text). A full flag whose prefix does not match --<plugin>- is rejected at registration and the plugin is reported as invalid. Dests are always <plugin>_<option> with dashes flipped to underscores (func-lain → --dorkbuilder-func-lain → dorkbuilder_func_lain), so a plugin can never shadow a core flag.

docs.title: PLUGIN keys
docs.text: Key Required Meaning name yes Matches ^[a-z][a-z0-9_-]{1,30}$; becomes the trigger flag. version no Shown by plugins list / plugins info. description no Help text for the trigger flag. options no List of option mappings (below).

docs.title: Option keys
docs.text: Key Meaning name Short name ([a-z][a-z0-9_-]*), auto-prefixed to --<plugin>-<name>. help Help text for the flag. type str (default), int, or float. choices Non-empty list of allowed string values. default Default value when the flag is absent. action "store_true" for a boolean switch (no type/choices).

docs.title: How a plugin runs
docs.text:
A plugin is triggered by either:

  1. the bare flag --<plugin> (store_true), or
  2. implicitly, when any --<plugin>-* argument appears on the command line.

Configuration defaults alone (plugins.options) never launch a plugin — only real command-line arguments do. Every triggered plugin runs in order and the first non-zero exit code wins.

atdork --dorkbuilder-list-types               # implicit: one option is enough
atdork --dorkbuilder --dorkbuilder-text "x"   # explicit trigger + option

Metadata is read with ast.literal_eval — listing and registering plugins never executes plugin code. A plugin module is imported and run only when it is actually triggered.

docs.title: ctx: what a plugin gets
docs.text:
run(args, ctx) receives the parsed namespace plus a PluginContext:

Attribute / method Purpose ctx.console Rich console for output. ctx.workspace Active environment, or None. ctx.package_dir Local package store directory. ctx.version AtDork version string. ctx.results_dir Environment results directory (or CWD). ctx.get_setting(key, default) Read a configuration value. ctx.guard_write(path) Resolve an output path through the environment write guard. ctx.search(query, **kwargs) Run one dork search through the normal AtDork engine.

Always write files through ctx.guard_write() — it enforces the active environment root and rejects paths that escape it.

docs.title: atdork plugins list
docs.text: Every discovered plugin with its version, status (ready, disabled, or invalid with the contract error), trigger flag, option count, and path.

docs.title: atdork plugins info <name>
docs.text: The full contract: version, description, source, path, install ref, status, and a table of every flag with its dest, type, default, and choices.

docs.title: atdork plugins run <name> [--opt KEY=VALUE]
docs.text:
Run a plugin without the flag syntax. Each --opt is coerced using the option's declared type. Handy for scripting:

atdork plugins run dorkbuilder --opt text=Acme --opt limit=3 --opt save=acme.txt

docs.title: Where plugins live
docs.text:
Discovery scans (later roots override earlier ones on a name collision):

  1. the package store <store>/plugins/ — populated by atdork install @plugins/<tool>;
  2. every folder listed in plugins.paths in your configuration (handy for local development).

A tool folder (@plugins/<tool>/) may contain helper _*.py files; only files with a valid PLUGIN literal become commands, and the rest are installed as supporting modules.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
version: 2
plugins:
  enabled: auto          # "auto" (all installed) or an explicit allow-list
  disabled: []           # plugin names to keep quiet
  paths: []              # extra local folders to scan
  options:               # per-plugin option defaults (CLI still wins)
    dorkbuilder:
      type: social-media

enabled accepts "auto" (default) or a list of names; disabled always wins. The section is validated fail-fast on load — unknown keys, wrong types, and malformed option defaults are rejected before anything runs. API keys and secrets are never stored in plaintext.

docs.title: Installing plugins
docs.text:
Plugins ship in the Atdork-DB repository under @plugins/:

atdork search dorkbuilder                 # find it
atdork install @plugins/dorkbuilder       # whole tool folder (plugin + helpers)
atdork install @plugins/dorkbuilder/dorkbuilder.py   # a single file
atdork plugins list                      # verify it's ready

docs.title: Installing from anywhere
docs.text:
Plugins do not have to come from Atdork-DB — a raw module, a git repo or a third-party registry work the same way:

# a single module URL (must end in .py)
atdork install https://raw.githubusercontent.com/user/repo/main/tool/tool.py

# a git repository: one plugin, or pick one with '#<subpath>'
atdork install https://github.com/user/atdork-plugins
atdork install https://github.com/user/atdork-plugins#my-tool
atdork install https://github.com/user/atdork-plugins#tools/my-tool
atdork install https://github.com/user/repo --git-ref v1.2.0   # pin a tag
atdork install "https://github.com/amnottdevv/Atdork-DB#@plugins/dorkbuilder"

# a third-party registry declared once in the config
atdork plugins sources                                     # list them
atdork install --source mine @plugins/my-tool

A registry is any repo that ships an Index.idn plus @plugins/<tool>/… folders — the same layout as Atdork-DB:

# atdork.yaml (or <env>/.config/config.yml)
plugins:
  sources:
    mine:
      url: https://github.com/user/atdork-plugins
      ref: main            # optional branch/tag
      index: Index.idn     # optional custom index path

Generate (or refresh) its index with:

atdork plugins publish @plugins/my-tool                  # print the lines
atdork plugins publish @plugins/my-tool --repo . --write # update Index.idn
git push   # your registry is now installable

Every external install goes through the same contract gate: metadata is read with AST (never executed), the name must match the plugin contract, files are size-capped, and registry installs verify every file against the checksum in that registry's Index.idn — a mismatch (or a missing sha256) aborts the install. Index entries are validated too: a ref that contains .. or an absolute path is rejected, and no install can write outside the local store.

docs.title: Available plugins
docs.text:
Plugin What it does dorkbuilder Build ready-to-run dork lists from text + a category reportgen Summarize result files into an HTML/JSON report subdomain Discover indexed subdomains of a target via search dorks emaildork Build (and optionally run) email-discovery dorks vulndork Vulnerability-hunting dork sets by target / product / CVE geodork Geographically-scoped dork builder usernamehunt Find where a username/handle is used across the web

Each tool ships with its own README.md. Browse them — with rendered READMEs, options and source links — in the web catalog's Plugins section.

docs.title: Security
docs.text:
Plugin metadata is parsed with ast.literal_eval — reading PLUGIN never executes code, so listing or registering plugins is side-effect free. A plugin module is imported only when one of its flags is actually triggered on the command line.

Because a triggered plugin is real Python that runs in your interpreter, the trust model is the package manager: only install plugins from a repository you trust (atdork install verifies the sha256 of every file against Index.idn). Treat installing a plugin like installing any other package.

Installing from a URL, a git repo or plugins.sources is TOFU trust: the checksum comes from that source, so adding a source means trusting everyone who can push to it. Prefer tags/commit-pinned registries for shared setups, and review a tool's code (atdork plugins info, the source link in the catalog) before running it.

Output writing goes through ctx.guard_write(), which enforces the active environment root — a plugin cannot write outside its workspace through the guarded path. Invalid plugins (bad metadata, wrong prefix, missing run()) are rejected at load time and reported by plugins list, never silently ignored.

Disable a plugin without uninstalling it via plugins.disabled in the configuration.

docs.title: AtDork Advanced Features Guide
docs.text: This document covers three powerful features that make AtDork a professional OSINT tool: Post‑Processing Hooks, Cache System, and Database & History.

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text: Post‑processing hooks allow you to run external commands on every URL discovered by AtDork. This is useful for automating vulnerability scanning, header grabbing, screenshotting, or any other action you want to perform on the results without manual effort.

docs.title: Functions
docs.text: Flag Description Default --exec "command {}" Execute a command for every result URL. {} is replaced with the URL. --exec-on-vuln "command {}" Execute only on URLs flagged as vulnerable (requires --filter-vuln). --exec-parallel N Number of parallel processes. 1 --exec-timeout N Timeout per command in seconds. 30

docs.title: Usage Examples
docs.text:
# Check HTTP headers of every discovered URL
atdork -q "inurl:admin" -r 10 --exec "curl -sI {} | grep Server"

# Run WPScan only on WordPress-related results
atdork -q "inurl:wp-content" -r 30 --filter-vuln wordpress \
  --exec-on-vuln "wpscan --url {} --enumerate p" --exec-parallel 3 --exec-timeout 60

# Save all URLs to a file for later use
atdork -q "site:example.com" -r 50 --exec "echo {} >> urls.txt"

docs.title: How It Works
docs.text:
1. After all results are collected and filtered, AtDork extracts the URL (href) from each result.
  2. If --exec-on-vuln is used, only URLs that pass the vulnerability filter are selected.
  3. The command template is filled by replacing {} with the (shell‑escaped) URL.
  4. Commands are executed using Python’s subprocess.run() in a thread pool (if --exec-parallel > 1).
  5. Stdout, stderr, return code, and any error are captured and logged.
  6. A short summary (success/failed/timeout) is printed after all commands finish.

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text: The cache system stores search results locally in a SQLite database. This prevents redundant requests to search engines, reduces bandwidth, and allows offline access to previously fetched results.

docs.title: Functions
docs.text: Flag Description Default --cache Enable caching. Every search result is saved and served from cache when possible. --cache-only Only use cached results; never contact search engines. --cache-ttl N Time‑to‑live in hours. Cached entries older than this are ignored. 24 --clear-cache Delete all cached entries before starting the session. --cache-db PATH Specify a custom cache database file. atdork_cache.db

docs.title: Usage Examples
docs.text:
# Cache all search results for 48 hours
atdork -q "site:gov filetype:pdf" -r 20 --cache --cache-ttl 48

# Use only cached data (offline mode)
atdork -q "site:gov filetype:pdf" -r 20 --cache-only

# Clear old cache and start fresh
atdork --clear-cache

# Use a custom cache location
atdork -q "test" --cache --cache-db /path/to/my_cache.db

docs.title: How It Works
docs.text:
1. A SearchCache object is created when any cache flag is used.
  2. A SQLite table api_cache is created (if not exists) with columns for query, engine, parameters (JSON), results (JSON), timestamps, and hit count.
  3. On cache write: after a successful search, the query, engine, normalized parameters, and the result list are stored with an expiration timestamp.
  4. On cache read: before a search, the cache is checked for an exact match (query + engine + params) that hasn’t expired. If found, the cached results are returned immediately.
  5. --cache-only skips the network call entirely and returns empty if no cache hit.
  6. --clear-cache deletes all rows from the table.
  7. Expired entries are automatically cleaned up on initialization.

The cache key is built from: - Query string - Backend engine - Parameters: region, safesearch, timelimit, max_results (all normalized to a sorted JSON string)

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text: AtDork can persistently store all queries and their results in a SQLite database. This enables resuming interrupted batches, viewing search history, deduplication across sessions, and exporting everything to JSON/CSV.

docs.title: Functions
docs.text: Flag Description Default --db-path PATH Database file path. atdork.db --resume Continue a previously interrupted batch (re‑runs queries with pending or failed status). --history Display a list of all previously executed queries with their status. --no-dedup Disable global URL deduplication (by default, duplicate URLs across queries are skipped). --export-db PATH Export the entire database to a JSON or CSV file (format guessed from extension).

docs.title: Usage Examples
docs.text:
# Resume an interrupted batch
atdork --resume

# View past searches
atdork --history

# Export all stored results to JSON
atdork --export-db all_results.json

# Export to CSV
atdork --export-db all_results.csv

# Disable deduplication (keep every URL even if seen before)
atdork -q "test" --no-dedup

# Use a custom database location
atdork --db-path /secure/path/atdork.db --history

docs.title: How It Works
docs.text:
1. A Database object is created from core/database.py. It manages two tables:
  2. queries (id, query_text, status, timestamps)

  3. results (id, query_id, title, href, body, raw_json, created_at) with a UNIQUE(query_id, href) constraint.

  4. During a batch or single search:

  5. Each query is inserted/updated with status pending → completed or failed.

  6. Results are inserted one by one; duplicates (same query_id + href) are silently ignored (unless --no-dedup).

  7. --resume:

  8. Reads all queries with status pending or failed, re‑executes them, and updates their status.

  9. --history:

  10. Prints all rows from the queries table with their status and timestamp.

  11. --export-db:

  12. Joins queries and results, then writes either a JSON (dict {query_id: [results]}) or a CSV (flat table with query_text, title, href, body).

  13. --no-dedup:

  14. When disabled, the add_result() method returns True only if a new row was actually inserted (using INSERT OR IGNORE and checking cursor.rowcount). The batch runner then counts only truly new results.

This database system makes AtDork suitable for long‑running engagements and professional reporting.

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text:
AtDork provides robust proxy management and anonymity features to protect your identity during OSINT operations. Whether you're using a single proxy, rotating through a pool, or routing through Tor, AtDork handles it all with strict mode to prevent IP leaks.

When enabled with --strict, AtDork will never fall back to a direct connection — it will fail cleanly rather than expose your real IP.

docs.title: What It Does
docs.text: Feature Description Proxy Rotation Rotate through multiple proxies automatically (HTTP, HTTPS, SOCKS4, SOCKS5) Tor Integration Route traffic through the Tor network with a single flag Strict Mode Fail completely if no proxy is available (no direct connection fallback) IP Leak Detection Detect and stop if your real IP is exposed (--ip-guard) Proxy Cooldown Temporarily ban failing proxies (configurable cooldown period) Auto-Removal Permanently remove proxies after N consecutive failures Proxy Statistics Track success/failure rates per proxy

docs.title: Single Proxy
docs.text: atdork -q "confidential filetype:docx" --proxy "http://user:pass@proxy:8080" --strict

docs.title: Multiple Proxies (Comma-Separated)
docs.text: atdork -q "target" --proxy "http://p1:8080,socks5://p2:1080" --strict

docs.title: Proxy File (Recommended for large scans)
docs.text:
atdork -q "target" --proxy-file proxies.txt --strict

Proxy file format (proxies.txt): 

# HTTP proxies
http://user:pass@dc1.provider.com:3128
http://user:pass@dc2.provider.com:3128

# SOCKS proxies
socks5://res1.provider.com:1080
socks5h://res2.provider.com:1080

# Comments with # are ignored

docs.title: Tor Integration
docs.text: atdork -q "target" --tor --strict

docs.title: With IP Guard (Leak Detection)
docs.text: atdork -q "target" --proxy-file proxies.txt --strict --ip-guard

docs.title: With Custom Proxy Settings
docs.text:
atdork -q "target" --proxy-file proxies.txt --strict \
  --proxy-cooldown 120 --max-failures 3

docs.title: 1. Proxy Manager (proxy_manager.py)
docs.text:
The Proxy Manager handles the entire proxy lifecycle:

Proxy Validation - Validates proxy format: scheme://[user:pass@]host:port - Automatically skips invalid proxies with a warning

Proxy Rotation - Rotates through proxies in a round-robin fashion - Skips proxies that are in cooldown (temporarily banned) - Returns None if all proxies are down and --strict is not set

Proxy Cooldown - When a proxy fails, it enters cooldown for the specified duration (default: 60s) - After cooldown, the proxy is tried again

Proxy Auto-Removal - Tracks consecutive failures per proxy - If a proxy fails --max-failures times consecutively, it's removed permanently (default: 3)

docs.title: 2. Proxy Selection Flow
docs.text:
1. User requests a proxy
   ↓
2. Proxy Manager checks the pool
   ↓
3. If proxy exists → return it
   ↓
4. If proxy fails → report_failure()
   ├─ Increment failure count
   ├─ Enter cooldown (--proxy-cooldown)
   └─ If max_failures reached → remove permanently
   ↓
5. Next request → get_proxy() skips cooldown proxies
   ↓
6. If all proxies are in cooldown and --strict=True → raise RuntimeError
   If --strict=False → return None (fallback to direct connection)

docs.title: 3. IP Guard (ip_guard.py)
docs.text:
When --ip-guard is enabled, AtDork actively monitors for IP leaks:

How It Works: 1. Establish Baseline: When the scan starts, IP Guard makes a test request through the proxy to determine the visible IP address 2. Periodic Checks: Every few queries, IP Guard rechecks the visible IP 3. Leak Detection: If the visible IP changes to your real IP (detected via httpbin.org/ip), AtDork stops immediately 4. Header Inspection: Checks response headers like X-Forwarded-For, CF-Connecting-IP, and X-Real-IP for your real IP

Panic Message Example: 

════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
  ❌  IP LEAK DETECTED – PROGRAM STOPPED

docs.title: 4. Tor Integration
docs.text:
AtDork integrates with Tor by connecting to the local SOCKS5 proxy:

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text:
The Resilience System is AtDork's intelligent fault‑tolerance engine. It ensures that large‑scale OSINT operations continue smoothly even when search engines block you, proxies fail, or network connections drop.

Activated with --resilient, it coordinates seven specialised modules under core/case/ to handle every failure scenario automatically.

docs.title: What It Does
docs.text: Scenario Without Resilience With Resilience Google returns HTTP 429 (Rate Limit) All subsequent queries fail Switches to Startpage, cools down Google for 120s Proxy dies mid‑batch Batch crashes Rotates to next healthy proxy All backends blocked Scan fails completely Falls back through 5+ search engines until one works Temporary network timeout Query fails permanently Retries up to 3x with exponential backoff Backend returns empty results Wastes retries on dead backend Immediately switches to next backend

  --proxy-file proxies.txt --strict --resilient \
  --concurrency 3 --format json -o recon.json

docs.title: 1. Error Classifier (error_classifier.py)
docs.text:
Classifies every exception into one of five categories:

Category Description Action TRANSIENT Timeout, connection reset Retry with backoff RATE_LIMIT HTTP 429, "too many requests" Switch backend, cooldown BLOCKED HTTP 403, CAPTCHA, "access denied" Switch backend + rotate proxy PROXY_FAIL Proxy dead, connection refused Rotate to next proxy FATAL Parsing error, bug Abort immediately

docs.title: 2. Circuit Breaker (circuit_breaker.py)
docs.text:
Prevents hammering dead backends/proxies. After a resource fails 3 times consecutively, the circuit opens.

Backend fails 3 times → Circuit OPEN for 120s
After 120s → HALF-OPEN: one request allowed
If succeeds → CLOSED (healthy again)
If fails → OPEN for another 120s

docs.title: 3. Fallback Manager (fallback_manager.py)
docs.text:
Decides the best action based on the error category and current state:

Error Category Decision RATE_LIMIT Switch to next healthy backend BLOCKED Switch backend + rotate proxy PROXY_FAIL Rotate proxy; if all proxies dead, cooldown TRANSIENT Retry same resource FATAL Abort with clear error

docs.title: 4. Retry Handler (retry_handler.py)
docs.text:
Implements exponential backoff with jitter to avoid overwhelming servers:

Attempt Delay (approx) 1st 2s 2nd 4s 3rd 8s

Jitter (random variance) prevents all threads from retrying at the exact same moment.

docs.title: 5. Adaptive Delay (adaptive_delay.py)
docs.text:
Adjusts delay per backend based on real‑time response codes:

  • Success (200 + results): Delay decreases by 10% (down to 0.1s minimum)
  • Rate limit (429): Delay doubles (up to 60s maximum)
  • Other errors: Delay unchanged

At the end of a batch, recommendations are displayed:

Rate Limiter Recommendations:
  google: 8/20 rate-limited. Increase delay to 5.0s or switch backend.
  startpage: 0/15 rate-limited. Everything healthy at 0.3s.

docs.title: 6. IP Guard (ip_guard.py)
docs.text:
When --strict is active, IP Guard periodically checks that your real IP is not being exposed:

  1. Establishes a baseline (IP visible through proxy/Tor)
  2. Checks every few queries that the visible IP hasn't changed to your real IP
  3. Inspects response headers (X-Forwarded-For, CF-Connecting-IP) for leaks
  4. If a leak is detected, AtDork halts immediately with a detailed panic message

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text:
AtDork's template system allows you to load pre-defined dork collections from YAML files. Instead of typing dorks manually or maintaining a text file, you can use curated templates for specific use cases like SQL injection discovery, WordPress vulnerability scanning, or exposed configuration file hunting.

Templates are YAML-based, support domain substitution with {target}, and can be combined with custom queries for maximum flexibility.

docs.title: What It Does
docs.text: Feature Description Curated Templates Pre-built dork collections for SQLi, XSS, LFI, WordPress, Joomla, and more Target Substitution Use {target} in dorks and replace with --target at runtime Selective Execution Run specific dorks from a template using --select (e.g., 1,3,5) Preview Mode See what dorks a template contains without executing them Custom Templates Create your own YAML templates and store them anywhere Template Listing List all available templates with descriptions

docs.title: 1. Template File Structure
docs.text:
Templates are YAML files with the following structure:

# wordlists/templates/sqli.yaml
name: sqli
description: SQL injection discovery dorks
category: vulnerability

# Dorks that require a target domain
targeted:
  - "site:{target} inurl:product.php?id="
  - "site:{target} inurl:category.php?id="
  - "site:{target} inurl:news.php?id="

# Generic dorks (no target needed)
generic:
  - "inurl:product.php?id="
  - "inurl:category.php?id="
  - "inurl:news.php?id="

docs.title: 2. Template Types
docs.text: Type Description When to Use targeted Contains {target} placeholder When you want to focus on a specific domain generic No placeholder, works everywhere For broad discovery across all domains

docs.title: 3. Detection Logic
docs.text:
1. User provides --template sqli --target example.com
   ↓
2. AtDork loads wordlists/templates/sqli.yaml
   ↓
3. Parses YAML:
   ├─ targeted: [dorks with {target}]
   └─ generic: [dorks without {target}]
   ↓
4. Renders dorks:
   ├─ targeted: replaces {target} with example.com
   └─ generic: kept as-is
   ↓
5. If --select provided:
   └─ Filters to specific indices (1,3,5)
   ↓
6. Executes all dorks as a batch
   └─ Same as --batch-file but generated dynamically

docs.title: 4. Example
docs.text:
Input Template (sqli.yaml): 

targeted:
  - "site:{target} inurl:product.php?id="
  - "site:{target} inurl:category.php?id="
generic:
  - "inurl:product.php?id="

Command: 

atdork --template sqli --target example.com --select 1

Generated Dorks: 

site:example.com inurl:product.php?id=

  • From Source: Templates are loaded from wordlists/templates/
  • Custom Templates: Use --template-path to load templates from any directory
  • Fail Closed: If a template is missing, AtDork exits with an error

Error Example: 

Template 'unknown' not found in 'wordlists/templates/'.
Use --list-templates to see the available list.

docs.title: Watch Mode
docs.text:
Watch mode monitors dorks for you: register a watch (a name plus the dorks to run), then run it as often as you like. Each run re-executes the dorks, compares the result URLs against the saved history, and reports only the new findings — on the console and, if configured, through your webhook (Notification: Discord, Slack, Telegram).

There is no daemon and no internal scheduler: one atdork watch run is exactly one cycle, which makes it a natural cron/systemd-timer job.

# 1. register a watch (stored in the environment)
atdork watch add acme \
    --dork "site:acme.com ext:env" \
    --dork "site:acme.com intitle:index.of" \
    --notify discord:https://discord.com/api/webhooks/…

# 2. first run records a baseline (no "new" spam)
atdork watch run acme

# 3. every later run reports the delta only
atdork watch run acme

Put step 3 in cron (each environment keeps its own watch state):

0 */6 * * *  cd /home/me && atdork --env ~/AtDork-workflows/atdork-env \
             watch run acme >> ~/atdork-watch.log 2>&1

Use atdork watch run --all to run every saved watch in one cycle.

docs.title: Dork sources
docs.text:
A watch can combine three kinds of sources — they are resolved on every run, so editing the file (or the Atdork-DB package) changes what is monitored without touching the watch:

Flag Source --dork "…" A literal dork (repeatable) --batch-file dorks.txt A file of dorks, one per line (repeatable) --database-dork @ghdb/01_footholds A database dork package spec (@folder/file, c@file.txt, whole folders) 
atdork watch add exposed-env \
    --database-dork @ghdb/01_footholds \
    --batch-file extra-dorks.txt \
    --max-results 30 --region us-en

Re-running watch add for an existing name merges: new dorks/files are appended, options and the webhook target are updated, and the seen-URL history is kept — so you never get re-notified about old findings.

docs.title: Commands
docs.text:
Command Description atdork watch add <name> [sources] [--notify TARGET] [options] Create (or extend) a watch. atdork watch list List watches with their source summary and last run. atdork watch show <name> Show the definition, stored options, history counters and the last new URLs. atdork watch run <name> Run one cycle (cron-friendly). atdork watch run --all Run every watch. atdork watch remove <name> Delete the watch and its history.

Stored search options (--backend, --max-results, --timeout, --retries, --delay, --region, --safesearch, --timelimit) are written into the watch on watch add (defaults come from your config) and can be overridden per run — atdork watch run acme --max-results 50 changes that cycle only.

Useful run flags:

Flag Effect --dry-run Resolve the dorks and exit — nothing is searched, no credits spent. --notify TARGET Override the stored webhook target for this cycle. --concurrency N Run N dorks in parallel. --all Run every watch and print a combined summary.

docs.title: How findings are detected
docs.text:
• Every result's link is normalized before comparison: scheme/host are lowercased, www. is dropped, a trailing slash and URL fragments are ignored, and known tracking parameters (utm_*, gclid, fbclid, …) are removed. http://WWW.Example.com/a/?utm_source=x and https://example.com/a count as the same finding.
  • The first run of a watch only records a baseline (and sends one short baseline notification, so you know the webhook works). Later runs report the delta.
  • The history is capped at 10,000 URLs per watch; the oldest entries are dropped first.
  • Watch runs deliberately never use the search cache — a monitored dork must be re-fetched to notice changes.

docs.title: State and exit codes
docs.text:
State lives in <env>/state/watch/<name>.json (or ~/.atdork/state/watch/<name>.json without an environment) and holds both the definition and the history — deleting the file resets the watch to a baseline state.

Exit code Meaning 0 Cycle completed (new findings, none, or some dorks failed). 1 The watch is unknown/invalid, or every dork failed. 2 watch run without a name and without --all.

Notification problems never fail a run: a dead webhook is logged and the cycle still exits 0 (its findings are already saved in the history).

docs.title: Workflows
docs.text:
Workflows turn AtDork from a single-search CLI into an orchestration tool: a workflow is a named, structured YAML definition that runs a series of dork steps strictly in order — AtDork finishes one command before moving to the next, exactly like chaining commands by hand, but with threshold retries, worker concurrency, guarded outputs, and resumable state.

workflows:
  recon-acme:
    target: "example.com"
    workers: 2
    steps:
      - name: exposed-files
        query: 'site:{target} ext:(pdf|docx) (intitle:index OR intitle:download)'
        when_results_below: 5
        retry_with:
          - 'site:{target} ext:pdf'
      - name: login-portals
        query: 'site:{target} inurl:(login OR signin)'

atdork workflow list                     # what's defined?
atdork workflow validate                 # schema check, zero API credits
atdork workflow run recon-acme           # execute
atdork --run-workflow .                  # one-shot: run the single workflow in the root

docs.title: Where definitions live
docs.text:
Workflow definitions are merged by name from (later wins):

  1. workflows: in any configuration layer (global ~/.config/atdork/config.yml, working-dir atdork.yaml, the active environment config, or --config);
  2. explicit files via --file / --workflow-file (repeatable);
  3. auto-discovered files named workflow.yaml, workflow.yml, workflows.yaml, workflows.yml, atdork-workflow.yaml or atdork-workflow.yml in the active environment root and the current working directory ("root"). The environment root wins on name collisions, mirroring the config layer order (env > CWD).

A standalone file uses the same shape as the config section:

version: 2
workflows:
  my-campaign:
    description: "..."        # shown by `workflow list`
    target: "example.com"
    steps:
      - name: first
        query: 'site:{target} inurl:login'

See examples/workflows/recon.yml for a fully commented example and the repository-root workflow.yaml demo.

docs.title: atdork workflow list
docs.text: Every workflow from the merged sources with its step count, source (config or file path) and description.

docs.title: atdork workflow validate [name]
docs.text:
Deep validation without spending a single request: schema, unknown keys, step names, substitution tokens, threshold/retry pairing, output formats, and whether every {target} usage has a target available. Exit code 1 on errors — safe for CI.

✗ broken — valid? no:
    workflows.broken.steps[0]: requires 'query' or 'queries'
    workflows.broken.steps[1].outputs[0]: format must be one of: csv, json, txt

docs.title: atdork workflow run <name>
docs.text:
<name> accepts three forms:

Form Meaning recon-acme Workflow name from config or a discovered file. ./my-workflow.yml File path — runs when the file holds exactly one workflow. . The single workflow discovered in the current root (error listing choices if there are several). Flag Description --file FILE Additional workflow YAML file(s), repeatable. --target TARGET Override the workflow-level target. --workers N Override the worker (thread) count of every step. --step NAME Run only this step. --resume Skip steps already recorded as completed. --dry-run Print the fully resolved queries; no search, no state written.

docs.title: One-shot main flags
docs.text:
The same engine is reachable without the subcommand:

atdork --run-workflow recon-acme --workflow-target example.org --workflow-workers 2
atdork --run-workflow . --workflow-dry-run
atdork --run-workflow recon-acme --workflow-resume
Flag Description --run-workflow NAME Workflow name, file path, or . (single workflow in the root). --workflow-file FILE Read definitions from this file. --workflow-target TARGET Override the target. --workflow-workers N Override the worker count. --workflow-resume Resume a previous run. --workflow-dry-run Resolve and print without searching.

docs.title: Workflow-level keys
docs.text: Key Type Description description string Shown by workflow list. target string Default target for {target} substitution (overridden by --target). workers int 1–64 Threads inside each step; steps themselves stay sequential. Default 1. steps list The step definitions, executed in order. on_error stop | continue Default failure policy for all steps. Default stop. worker_overrides mapping Search kwargs merged on top of every step's kwargs (see below). search keys Workflow-wide defaults for any step search kwarg: backend, max_results, region, safesearch, timelimit, timeout, retries, delay, user_agent, verify, fallback_backends, fallback_chain, forced_proxy.

docs.title: Step keys
docs.text:
Key Type Description name string Unique per workflow; defaults to step-1, step-2, ... query string The dork to run (mutually exclusive with queries). queries list Several dorks in one step — distributed across workers. when_results_below int Threshold: fewer unique results → run retry_with. retry_with list Alternate queries executed when the threshold is missed; their results are merged and deduplicated into the step results. on_error stop | continue Overrides the workflow-level policy for this step. outputs list Result files: - file: path.json + optional format: txt\|json\|csv. worker_overrides mapping Search kwargs applied on top for this step. search keys Any workflow-level search key, overridden for this step.

Search kwargs precedence: workflow defaults → step keys → worker_overrides (workflow-level, then step-level) — later wins. This is how one step can force an API backend while the rest of the campaign scrapes:

steps:
  - name: portals
    query: 'site:{target} inurl:login'
    worker_overrides:
      backend: serper     # requires engines.serper.api_key (see Engines)

docs.title: Substitution
docs.text:
Token Value {target} The resolved target (--target > workflow target). {step} Current step name. {date} Run date, YYYYMMDD. {run_id} Short id of this run (stable across --resume).

Available in queries, retry_with, output paths and description-adjacent strings. Unknown tokens fail validation with a typo-friendly error; literal braces such as ext:{pdf,docx} are never treated as tokens.

docs.title: Sequential steps, concurrent queries
docs.text: Steps always run in order: step N+1 starts only after N finished. Inside a step, workers: N runs that step's queries (queries: lists or retry_with batches) on N threads — the same thread pool machinery as --concurrency, so caching, dedup and the circuit breaker all apply.

docs.title: Threshold retries (when_results_below + retry_with)
docs.text:
After the step's primary queries finish, unique results (deduplicated by URL) are counted. Below the threshold → each retry_with query runs in order, and all results merge into the step's output. The step is then marked:

Status Meaning done Threshold met (or no threshold configured). below_threshold Finished, but still fewer unique results than requested. Recorded; the run continues. failed All queries of the step failed (backend errors exhausted) — on_error decides whether the run stops.

A below_threshold step is not an error: campaigns against small targets legitimately return little.

docs.title: Failure policy (on_error)
docs.text:
• stop (default): the first failed step aborts the remaining steps — fast, deterministic, and re-runnable with --resume.
  • continue: later steps still run; the summary lists the failure.

Step-level errors (including output paths rejected by the environment write guard) are recorded the same way — a workflow never crashes mid-run with a half-written state.

docs.title: State and --resume
docs.text:
Every run persists a JSON state file:

<environment root>/state/workflows/<name>.json    # env active
~/.atdork/state/workflows/<name>.json             # no env

It records the run_id, per-step status, result counts and written outputs. --resume (or --workflow-resume) skips steps whose status is done or below_threshold and re-runs only failed/missing steps under the same run_id. Without --resume a run starts fresh and overwrites the state.

--dry-run never writes state and never calls a search backend — use it to preview the exact queries a campaign would execute.

docs.title: Outputs and the environment guard
docs.text:
Each step may write its merged results:

outputs:
  - file: recon/files.json    # relative → inside the environment root/results
    format: json
  • Formats: txt, json, csv (default: inferred from the extension).
  • Relative paths resolve against <env>/results/ when an environment is active, else the working directory.
  • With an active environment every output goes through the strict write guard: paths escaping the root fail the step — results cannot leak outside the workspace.

docs.title: Backends, API providers and credit caution
docs.text: Workflows use the normal search machinery: backend accepts scraping backends, API engines (serper, serpapi, brave) and profiles: names; fallback_chain/search.fallback and the --resilient circuit breaker apply per query. Each step query counts against your API quota — run --dry-run first, keep max_results sane, and prefer scraping backends for exploratory steps with API backends reserved for worker_overrides on the steps that need them.

docs.title: Complete example
docs.text:
version: 2
workflows:
  recon-acme:
    description: "Full recon sweep for one target"
    target: "example.com"
    workers: 2
    max_results: 50
    region: "us-en"
    steps:
      - name: exposed-files
        query: 'site:{target} ext:(pdf|docx) (intitle:index OR intitle:download)'
        when_results_below: 10
        retry_with:
          - 'site:{target} ext:pdf'
          - 'site:{target} (filetype:doc OR filetype:xls)'
        outputs:
          - file: recon/files.json
            format: json

      - name: login-portals
        queries:
          - 'site:{target} inurl:(login OR signin OR admin)'
          - 'site:{target} intitle:"index of" (.env OR .git)'
        worker_overrides:
          backend: serper
        on_error: continue

      - name: fingerprints
        query: 'site:{target} ("wordpress" OR "drupal") inurl:wp-admin'
        outputs:
          - file: recon/fingerprints.csv
            format: csv

atdork workflow validate recon-acme
atdork workflow run recon-acme --dry-run
atdork workflow run recon-acme                 # fresh run
atdork workflow run recon-acme --resume        # after a stop/failure

docs.title: Tips
docs.text:
• Validate in CI: atdork workflow validate exits non-zero on bad definitions — catch typos before they burn API credits.
  • Environments: pair workflows with atdork env create so every result file, cache entry and state file stays inside one portable folder.
  • Combine with packages: queries: can reference installed dork files via --database-dork-style content only in plain text — copy the dorks into queries: or generate a workflow with a small script.
  • Debug a step in isolation: --step <name> runs a single step under the workflow's own configuration.
